Build a personal brand on X in three steps. Use this when starting or resetting a personal or founder account on X and you need a repeatable plan: niche and profile, a content-pillar funnel mix, and a posting and packaging routine.
Build an X account that earns reach, trust and conversions, using a three-step crash course: craft the brand, set content pillars, execute content.

- [YOUR_SKILLS] and the hot niches you could serve ([NICHE_CANDIDATES])
- [OFFER_OR_PRODUCT_LINK] (optional)
- Time budget per post, which decides the posting strategy in step 3

1. Find your pocket. Overlap a hot niche (the video's examples: AI, tech, startups, crypto) with your skills. The overlap is your pocket.
2. Pick audience pain points. Ask what your younger self (the video says 16) would want to consume to upskill in this niche.
3. Study the top 10 to 20 accounts in the niche (the video uses an AI assistant to list them). For each, note: formats (articles, threads, videos), messaging (how they package hooks and address pain points), and gaps. Find gaps by reading their comments for critiques and questions, then turn those into your own content.
4. Profile basics:
   - Bio: three lines at most, just say what you do.
   - Profile picture: your real face (the video claims this beats 80% of the competition; unverified).
   - Banner: a plain colour or a simple quote.
   - CTA (optional): a link to a product in the bio, not contact details.

5. Treat X as top of funnel: generate impressions fast and send people to other platforms (the video's example: YouTube).
6. Split content roughly: 60 to 70% top of funnel (trends, viral posts, infographics, news, broad niche topics), about 30% trust and personal (personal takes, videos), about 10% conversion (product or off-platform offer, never pushy).

7. Be value-driven: how-tos and full guides, plus "only you can say" posts drawn from your own network and experience. Skip aimless takes.
8. Own a niche: don't copy existing accounts; define a specific category.
9. Show proof: impressions generated, case studies, a video of you talking to a client about their pain points.
10. Pick one posting strategy and don't mix them:
   - Quality: 3 to 5 posts a day, at least 3 hours apart, about 3 hours of work per post.
   - Quantity: up to 24 posts a day, at least 1 hour apart, for news-style or fast niches. Higher flop risk.

11. Package each post: a curiosity-gap hook, a clear CTA that tells people exactly what to do (the video's example: "We work with founders that are struggling to write content. DM me this word..."), and a mix of formats across long and short video and long and short written posts. [HOOK_EXAMPLES: the video gives none; add your own.]

- Negativity: politics and hate on other creators; reports and mutes hurt reach. Block haters instead.
- Reply-guy spam.
- AI slop: low-effort AI-generated replies.

- Profile, niche statement and the three-bucket content mix are written down.
- A posting strategy is chosen and followed for a set period ([REVIEW_PERIOD]), then reviewed against impressions and conversions. (added, not in source)

- Automated posting or reply bots.
- Paid growth or audience purchases.
- Treating the percentages and frequencies as proven; they are the author's opinion.

Build a production agent on Claude Managed Agents. Use this when you are designing or building a hosted, long-running Claude agent (Claude Managed Agents, the Agent SDK, or your own harness) and need the architecture, multi-agent setup, scheduling, memory, credential handling, evals and multi-customer layout right.

chunks.section: 1. Design: split session, brain and hands
chunks.text:
1. Keep three separate parts, never one container:
   - **Session**: an append-only log of every event. The only durable piece; protect it.
   - **Brain**: the harness (tool loop, context management) plus the model. Replaceable.
   - **Hands**: sandboxes, MCP servers, tools. Provisioned on demand, discarded after.
2. Recovery rules:
   - Sandbox dies: return it to the model as a failed tool call; let it reprovision or continue.
   - Harness dies: start a new one, read the session log, resume from the last event.
3. Never rewrite the log for compaction. Compaction only picks what goes into context (summary, last N events), so you can change the strategy later.
4. Start inference before any sandbox exists; spawn a sandbox only when the model needs one. One container per task to limit blast radius.

chunks.section: 1. Design: split session, brain and hands
chunks.text: 5. Write down the harness's model-specific assumptions (for example a context reset for a model that rushes near its context limit). Re-check them, with evals, on every model change and delete what's no longer needed.

6. Credentials never enter the sandbox. Put a placeholder there; a proxy or vault swaps in the real secret at egress, only for hosts allowed for that secret. In Claude Managed Agents: create a vault, add secrets (env vars, MCP OAuth), pass the vault ID on the session.
7. Restrict environment networking to the domains and MCP servers the agent needs. Unrestricted is for demos only.

chunks.section: 3. Build the basic agent (Claude Managed Agents API)
chunks.text:
8. Create an **environment**: sandbox template, networking rules, packages (installed once at creation, cached; must come from public registries, uploaded files, or attached GitHub repos).
9. Create an **agent**: name, model, system prompt, tools (start with the default agent toolset: read, write, grep and similar).
10. Create a **session** with `<AGENT_ID>` and `<ENVIRONMENT_ID>`. It idles until it gets an event.
11. Talk over the event stream: send `user.message`; handle custom tool use events and return custom tool results; watch for idle, errors and interrupt. For a UI, have your backend listen to the SSE stream and re-stream to the browser.
   - Shortcut: Console > Managed Agents > Quick Start, describe the agent in one sentence, review the proposed prompt, model and tools.

12. Add **skills** for domain procedures (for example how to call `<DATA_SOURCE>` and its required identity). Skills are live: new sessions pick up edits.
13. Add **sub-agents** with their own prompts, tools and permissions, plus a reference to the main agent itself so it can spawn a copy when no specialist fits. Sub-agents get the prompt, tools and schemas, not the parent transcript, so put all needed context in the delegation.
14. Attach a **memory store** shared across sessions (several can attach, e.g. user-level plus org-wide). Instruct the agent to check memory first and not redo known work.

15. For long async jobs use **Outcomes**: task, rubric, max iterations. A verifier sub-agent grades against the rubric and the agent retries until it passes. Rubrics apply at session level only. Ask for deliverables in a fixed file location and structured format (e.g. a JSON scorecard plus a memory note).
16. Fan out with a custom tool (e.g. `dispatch_<WORKERS>`) that your app server handles by starting one session per item, then aggregating. Each child session keeps its own sub-agents, outcome and memory.
17. Keep the coordinator chatty: put human-in-the-loop or other blocking custom tools on a sub-agent, not the main thread.
18. For a team chat (Slack-like): one session per thread, prefix each `user.message` with who said it, give the agent an explicit post tool instead of mirroring every reply.

19. Recurring work is a **deployment**: agent, schedule (`<CRON>`), initial messages, attached memory stores, repos or files. Each fire creates a session; you can also trigger a run on demand via API. Memory is shared only where you attach it.
20. **Dreaming** (research preview): pick a memory store, a model, optional instructions and a time window of past sessions (e.g. 30 days). It reviews those transcripts and updates the memory store (e.g. notes on gaps in a skill). Run your own evals before trusting the update; a majority of sessions can agree on a wrong lesson.

21. Build an eval set from historical sessions and their results; data quality matters more than tooling. Rerun it after any model, prompt or harness change. Run datasets as many parallel sessions.
22. Code review in CI: on each PR, start one or more sessions with sub-agents to review the diff; optionally run the app in the sandbox and have the agent QA it with a browser.
23. Multi-tenant layout:
    - Don't use end users' own API keys; you lose observability.
    - Keep the agent definition as YAML in your repo and sync it to every workspace through CI.
    - Legal data separation: one workspace (or org) per customer. Otherwise one workspace with per-customer agents, or one shared agent with `customer_id` in session metadata.
    - Everything in a workspace is visible to all its members and keys; enforce finer access in your app.
24. Observability: consume the full event stream (console transcript and debug views, or the events API) and export it yourself. Add a status-update tool for long runs if humans need progress.

- Killing the harness or sandbox mid-task loses no work.
- The model never sees a real token.
- A long job ends with the rubric passed, the deliverable in its set location and memory updated.
- Evals pass after each model or harness change.

- One container holding log, harness and sandbox (a "pet" you can't lose or debug).
- Secrets inside the sandbox or in the prompt.
- Rewriting the event log when compacting.
- Expecting sub-agents to know the parent's conversation.
- Blocking the main coordinator on a custom tool.
- Trusting dreamed memory updates without evals.
- Mixing customers who need legal separation in one workspace.
- Hard-coding a fixed sub-agent topology when the model can choose; the speakers say letting it choose did better (no figures given).
- Assuming spend caps, session rewind or fork, sub-agent-level rubrics, fine-grained access control, non-Claude models, Bedrock or on-prem exist; none did at the time of the talk.

Build an AI hook bank from saved TikToks. Use this when you need a repeatable hook system for social/YouTube — save hooks while scrolling (especially TikTok), extract them into one DB with Louise’s Claude skill (github.com/louisedesadeleer/tiktok-hooks), then remap emotional structures onto product content without letting AI write the final line.

chunks.section: Build an AI hook bank from saved TikToks (Tella / Louise method)
chunks.text: Build a swipe-file of high-performing hooks (especially from TikTok), auto-extract spoken + visual hooks into one database with a Claude skill, then remap the emotional structure onto content that sells your product — without letting AI write the final hook.

- Tella YouTube: ~300 views → ~30,000 views after Louise owned hooks + content
- Principle: the hook is ~80% of whether a piece of content works
- TikTok partner guidance (via Carmen Vicente): spend ≥50% of content effort on the hook
- Personal brand: occasional viral post can add ~2–3k followers at once

- Hardest platform to hold attention → if a hook holds 5–10+ seconds there, the framework is strong
- Short-form reps: many hooks per scroll vs one YouTube cold open
- B2B buyers (CMOs, founders) are still humans on consumer apps; transfer TikTok/IG patterns to X, LinkedIn, YouTube
- Use fear/emotion carefully on brand accounts; founder accounts can be looser

- Claude subscription (Claude Code / terminal easiest)
- Hook collection folders on TikTok (recommended), plus X / LinkedIn / IG as available
- Destination DB: Obsidian Bases, Notion, or a local markdown file
- Free skill repo: https://github.com/louisedesadeleer/tiktok-hooks

chunks.section: 1. Build the swipe file while you scroll
chunks.text:
1. Create a **Hooks** collection/folder on each platform you use (TikTok first).
2. When something *actually* stops you for 5–10+ seconds or creates a visceral reaction (spoken line, on-screen text, or visual open), save it immediately — don’t overthink.
3. Optional parallel folders: e.g. **video inspiration** for full structure, not just opens.
4. Prefer saves with a clear **spoken hook**; visual-only opens still help for pattern notes.

1. Paste `https://github.com/louisedesadeleer/tiktok-hooks` into Claude Code (or Claude chat: “install this skill / what do I do with this?”).
2. Let it walk the install (may require terminal commands for local deps / browser cookies).
3. Prefer terminal / Claude Code for reliability.

When prompted by the skill:

1. **Where hooks live** → Obsidian vault, Notion, or a local markdown file.
2. **Sync private TikTok collection?** → Yes → paste the **web URL of your Hooks collection**.
3. **How many** → start with 5–20 recent saves (first sync imports the configured initial count, not the full backlog).
4. **View** → spreadsheet / Bases-style DB with thumbnail when possible.

Target columns in the swipe file:

| Column | What goes here |
| --- | --- |
| Spoken hook | First spoken sentence / cold open |
| Visual hook | On-screen text / first-frame pattern |
| Concept | Underlying emotion or framework (fear, guilt-relief, X vs Y, etc.) |
| Source | Link to the original video |
| Your idea | Blank — your remapped angle for your product |

What the skill does under the hood:

- Reads TikTok login cookies from your browser locally

- Downloads + transcribes on your machine (scripted — not flaky pure browser-use)
- Pulls early spoken lines as the hook + first-frame / on-screen visual cue
- Dedupes and appends into your DB; optional daily sync / launchd scheduling
- Does not keep downloaded videos after processing

Optional: hand the same skill to an always-on agent to ingest **new** saves on a cron.

chunks.section: 4. Turn banked hooks into content that sells (human final pass)
chunks.text:
1. Start from **product / offer**, then wander as far from pure product spam as you can while staying relevant.
2. Open the hook DB; pick a row that still creates a **visceral** reaction.
3. Extract the **template**, not the topic:
   - Emotion (guilt, fear, relief, curiosity, status)
   - Structure (e.g. “If X makes you uncomfortable, it doesn’t mean you’re Y”)
   - Contrast / timeline patterns (“how we used to do X vs how we do it now”)
4. Remap onto your buyer’s pain and your product’s job-to-be-done.
5. **Do not ship AI’s final wording** — Louise calls AI-written final hooks “cooked” (cliché, flat). Claude is great at scraping, transcribing, structuring, and reminding you of frameworks from your local DB; the last line is yours.
6. Ship across channels; reuse the same hook skeleton for short video, LinkedIn, X, and YouTube opens.

- **YouTube**: mix keyword/SEO with fast trend rides (watch X for model drops → ship related tut within 1–2 weeks); add **series** for return visits
- **LinkedIn / X**: worldview and founder voice; video still an edge in B2B
- Attribution is messy (dark social); still treat hook craft as the main lever for reach

chunks.section: Example hooks from the walkthrough (for pattern recognition)
chunks.text:
- Fear / timely: “When all the AI companies are about to IPO, your economic bells should go off.”
- Guilt-relief structure: “If doing X makes you uncomfortable, that doesn’t mean you’re cold / ungrateful / a bad [role]…”
- Visual how-to: big on-screen text like “how to get better at being judged”
- Contrast / judgment: “Shopping is the lowest form of self-expression.”

- Hooks folders exist and get regular saves
- Skill installed; DB filling with spoken + visual hooks + concept + blank “your idea”
- You’ve remapped banked hooks onto product content
- You’re no longer stuck for opens; AI suggestions are structure prompts, not final copy

- Scrolling without saving
- Letting Claude write the final hook (“cooked” copy)
- Only talking about the product
- Overusing fear-based hooks on corporate brand accounts
- Relying on browser-use alone to download every TikTok
- Expecting clean form-fill attribution for organic content

Build an MCP App plugin for Google Antigravity. Use this when building an MCP tool or plugin that should show an interactive HTML view in Google Antigravity (inline in chat, side panel, full page or a custom file viewer) while still working as plain text in clients without UI support.

chunks.section: Build an MCP App plugin for Google Antigravity
chunks.text:
An MCP App is an MCP tool that sends back an interactive HTML view as well as plain text. Antigravity implements the open MCP Apps spec (`io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`) and adds its own extension (`com.google.antigravity/ui`) for three extra places a view can open: a side panel, a full page and a custom file viewer. This skill follows Google's Antigravity docs page.

Use an MCP App when you need a reusable interface backed by a live MCP server, a side-panel view or a custom file viewer. For a one-off chart, diagram or prototype in a single conversation, use Antigravity's `/generative_ui` command instead.

- `<PLUGIN_NAME>`: the plugin's name.
- `<SERVER_NAME>`: the MCP server's name.
- What each view should do.
- Local `stdio` server or remote Streamable HTTP server (`<SERVER_URL>`).
- For a file viewer, the file extensions it claims (`<.EXT>`).

1. Pick where each view appears. A tool sets this in its `_meta`.
   - Inline in chat: `_meta.ui.resourceUri` only. The view replaces the collapsed tool-step card and grows to fit, up to 800 px tall (150 px if it never reports a size).
   - Side panel: add an `aux_pane` entrypoint. It opens beside the conversation when the agent calls the tool, or from the Plugins menus. There's one tab per server and tool pair, and later agent calls update the open tab in place.
   - Full page: add a `global` entrypoint. It opens full-width from Plugins in the left sidebar. Conversation-only actions (`message`, `updateModelContext`) aren't available here.
   - File viewer: add a `file` entrypoint with `extensions`. It replaces the built-in viewer for those file types.
   - A tool that has an `aux_pane` or `global` entrypoint doesn't render inline.

2. Scaffold. In the Antigravity App you can ask the built-in command to do it. The docs' example prompt:
   ```
   /mcp-app-development Build an MCP App plugin for Antigravity that tracks release checklist items inline in chat and in a side panel board using @modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps.
   ```
   To build it by hand instead, carry on to step 3.
3. Build the view as a single HTML file, served as a `ui://<SERVER_NAME>/<VIEW>.html` resource with MIME type `text/html;profile=mcp-app`. Link it from the tool's `_meta.ui.resourceUri`. Use the `@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps` SDK for the iframe bridge.
4. Always return clear plain text in `content` as well as `structuredContent`. Antigravity's CLI, its IDE and other MCP clients without UI support run the same tools as plain-text tools and never mount the view.

6. For file viewers, read and write through the host rather than the server.
   - Read: from the iframe, send `resources/read` for the exact `resourceUri` you were given. Antigravity answers directly with a base64 blob of up to 10 MiB.
   - Write (local files only): check `hostContext["com.google.antigravity/resources"]?.write` before showing save controls. If it's there, send `com.google.antigravity/resources/write` with `{ uri, text }` or `{ uri, blob }`, up to 10 MiB.
7. Optional host actions.
   - Open a file in the side panel: call `app.request()` with method `com.google.antigravity/toggle-aux-pane` and params `{ "tabType": "fileView", "uri": "file:///<PATH>" }`. Handle error `-32601` on hosts that don't support it.
   - Start a background conversation: pass `_meta: { "com.google.antigravity/message": { "target": "new" } }` in `app.sendMessage()`.

8. Package it as a plugin with `mcp_config.json` at the plugin root.
   - For a local `stdio` server, use `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` and `${PLUGIN_DATA}` in paths.
   - For a remote server, use `serverUrl`.
   - Antigravity falls back to its bundled Node.js only when `"command": "node"`.
9. Validate and install locally with `agy plugin validate --strict`, then `agy plugin install <PLUGIN_PATH>`.
10. Iterate.
    - HTML changes apply when you close and reopen the view, because `ui://` resources are fetched fresh each time the view mounts.
    - After changing local server code, restart the server: Customizations > Installed > the plugin > MCP > More actions > Restart.

- HTML and file reads or writes: 10 MiB.
- Stored tool result: 1 MiB. Load larger data through a tool only the app can call.
- Up to 4 tool calls at once per view, only to the server that owns the view. Calls still running when the view closes are cancelled.
- Up to 5 hidden side-panel or full-page frames stay loaded. After that, the least recently used one is dropped.
- No teardown notice is sent when a view closes.
- The iframe is isolated, with no persistent browser storage. Everything is blocked by default: allowlist bare origins only, in `_meta.ui.csp`.

- `agy plugin validate --strict` passes.
- Each view opens on the surface it declared.
- A UI-less client (the `agy` CLI) gets useful plain text from every tool.

(Check added, not in source.)

- Returning only `structuredContent`. Clients without UI support get nothing useful.
- Putting a `file` entrypoint on a model-callable tool. The whole tool is hidden from the model.
- Relying on teardown to save edits. Nothing is sent when a view closes, so save every edit as soon as it's made.
- Opening network access with `connectDomains` when a `tools/call` would do.
- Treating `visibility: ["app"]` as a security boundary. The `agy` CLI ignores it and shows every tool to the model. (Inference added, not in source.)
- Returning datasets over 1 MiB straight from a tool result.
- Letting a skill or plugin override a bot's own approval or send rules. It can't. (Added, not in source.)

Build and test small Roblox games with Claude. Use this when making simple Roblox games to earn from players: picking an open genre, getting Claude to write the scripts one system at a time, running a small ad test, then killing or scaling each game.

chunks.section: Build and test small Roblox games with Claude
chunks.text:
Make simple Roblox games with Claude writing the scripts. Ship each one, test it with a small ad spend, then kill it or scale it. Each new game reuses scripts from the last one.

Inputs: Roblox Studio, Claude, about 1 hour a day, and $50–100 ad budget per game.

1. Find a genre that's still open.
   - Open Roblox's Charts and look at Up-and-Coming.
   - Look for games under 3 months old with 1,000+ players.
   - New games breaking into a genre means it's still open. If the top 10 are all 5 years old, skip that genre.
2. Play the top 3 games in that genre for 10 minutes each.
   - Write down everything that's slow, confusing or boring.
   - That list is your game design. You're building the same kind of game without the annoying parts.
3. Describe your game in one sentence.
   - Too vague: "an obby."
   - Good: "escape a cage that gets harder every level, with friends."
   - If you can't explain it in one sentence, players won't get it in 10 seconds.
4. Get a build plan from Claude (about 15 minutes).
   - Give Claude the one-sentence idea and your list of fixes.

- Ask for a build plan split into small systems: movement, levels, UI, saving, shop.
   - The plan is your to-do list.
   - Example prompt (added, not in source; the post gives no wording):
     ```
     Game idea: <ONE_SENTENCE_IDEA>
     Problems to fix from the top games in this genre: <FIX_LIST>
     Write a build plan for this Roblox game, split into small systems I can build one per session: movement, levels, UI, saving, shop. For each system, list what it does and how I'll test it in Studio.
     ```
5. Build one system per session.
   - Claude writes the script. You paste it into Studio and test it.
   - If something breaks, paste the error back to Claude to fix.
   - At an hour a day, expect 2–3 weeks for a simple game. The author's fastest went from first line of code to live in under 24 hours.
6. Spend extra time on the first 30 seconds.

- Most players decide straight away whether to stay.
   - Give them a clear goal and fast action, with no confusing menus.
   - The author says an hour here is worth more than an hour on any other part of the game.
7. Make a thumbnail people want to click.
   - Study the thumbnails of the top 5 games in your genre.
   - Match their style and colours, but make it your own.
   - On Roblox the thumbnail is your ad. A great game with a bad thumbnail gets no players.
8. Add ways to earn before launch, then test.
   - Game passes.
   - In-game items and boosts.
   - Rewarded video ads.
   - Publish, put $50–100 into Roblox ads, and watch for 3–5 days.
9. Kill it or scale it.
   - If players leave fast, drop the game and start the next one.
   - If players stay and come back, push updates and spend more on ads.
10. Repeat in the same genre.

- The next game reuses about half the scripts from the last one, so each game gets quicker to build.
    - Hits fade over time, so keep shipping.

- A one-sentence pitch and a fix list exist before any code is written.
- Every system was tested in Studio before the next one was started.
- After the 3–5 day ad test, there's a written kill-or-scale decision based on whether players stayed and came back.

- His game made $778 in one day with 3,000 players. He works that out as about 26 cents per player.
- He then says a small game that "holds 100 players" makes about $26 a day, or $780 a month, so 10 such games make $7,800 a month.
- Treat this as a claim. It's one game's best day. "3,000 players" and "holds 100 players" probably measure different things (players in a day versus players online at once), so the maths may not carry over. He sells a course, linked at the end of the thread.

- Inventing a new genre instead of improving one that's already working.
- Picking a genre where the top 10 games are years old.
- Building the whole game in one go instead of one tested system at a time.
- Launching with no way to earn, or with a thumbnail you didn't study.
- Holding on to a game that players leave quickly.
- Planning around $7,800 a month. The post itself says not every game will hit.

Build motion-graphics videos with Claude Code. Use this when making launch promos, product updates, tweet-to-video or website-to-video motion graphics with a coding agent and an HTML or React video framework.

1. Use Claude Code (or a similar agent that writes code, runs it and reviews the output) with the strongest model and high reasoning. The source used Opus 5.5.
2. Pick a framework that renders code to MP4:
   - HyperFrames (HTML to MP4, open source from HeyGen): `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`, then `npx hyperframes init my-video && cd my-video`. Slash commands: `/hyperframes`, `/hyperframes-cli`, `/gsap`.
   - Remotion (React): `npx skills add remotion-dev/skills`, then `npx create-video@latest`.
3. Smoke test: "Using /hyperframes, create a 5-second video where the words 'Hello World' animate in one at a time on a cream background." If you get an MP4 back, you're set.
4. Run the first few videos in Plan Mode so scenes are mapped out before any code, which saves wasted renders.

Create `.claude/skills/brand-motion/SKILL.md`:
```
---
name: brand-motion
description: Brand rules for every motion video. Use for any video, animation, or motion graphic.
---
Primary [#hex]; Secondary [#hex]; Accent [#hex], used sparingly for the one thing that matters most; Background [#hex]
Headlines [font, weight]; Body [font, weight]. Never more than two fonts per video.
File: assets/logo.svg. Always use the real file, never redraw it. Clear space [X]px. Never stretch, recolour, or animate it in pieces.

We move like: [confident and precise / warm and playful / calm and premium]
Primary motion: damped springs, slight overshoot, quick settle
Transitions: [e.g. hard cuts on the beat]
Never: [bouncy cartoon motion / spinning / glitch effects]

Every video ends on [logo + tagline / CTA], held [X] seconds.
```

```
ROLE: You are a senior motion designer and creative developer at a world-class studio. Your work is meticulously art-directed, never template-looking.
FORMAT: Length [15]s, aspect [16:9 / 9:16 / 1:1], [30] fps, framework [/hyperframes or Remotion]
GOAL: [one sentence on what the viewer should feel or do]
SCENES: Scene 1 ([0:00-0:03]): [what's on screen, what moves, how] ... final scene: end card, CTA, logo
VISUAL STYLE: palette [#hex...], background [colour/texture], references [attached images and what to take from each]
TYPOGRAPHY: font [name]; headlines [weight, size, enter/exit]; body [weight, size]
MOTION LANGUAGE: feel [snappy / smooth / playful]; transitions [how scenes hand off]. Every element moves with intent.
AUDIO: music [file, BPM]; sync [which moments land on which beats]; SFX [where, sparingly]
DO NOT: generic fade-ins or default easing; stock gradients or glows; more than [X] words on screen; [other]
PROCESS: Plan the full sequence before writing code. Show me the scene plan first, then build.
```
Shortcut: describe the video in plain English, have Claude interview you one question at a time, then fill in this template.

- **Pacing:** one idea per scene, vary the rhythm, give the track's BPM and say where to cut, and go easy on sound effects. Claude's default output runs slow.
- **Real assets only:** put logo SVGs, font files, screenshots and audio in `assets/` and reference them by name. Never let it redraw a logo, guess a font, or invent a screenshot.
- **Scene by scene:** give exact timestamps for every scene.

- **Launch promo, 15s:** problem as kinetic type (0-4s), then product screenshots as floating UI cards with a zoom on [key feature] (4-11s), then logo and CTA end card held 2s. Transitions should feel connected, never like separate slides.
- **Talking-head intro:** transcribe `assets/clip.mp4`, add key-word captions only, [2-3] overlays at set moments with sparing sound effects, never cover the face, and a 2s animated title. Show the caption plan and overlay timings before building.
- **Tweet to video, 12s, 1:1:** avatar and handle slide in, text builds line by line with the key phrase in the accent colour, then settles into a readable card. Don't recreate the X interface or logo. Say which phrase gets emphasis before building.

- **Website to video, 20s, 16:9:** screenshot the hero, features and CTA, and pull the real colours, fonts, logo and copy with nothing invented. Headline as kinetic type, three feature cards, then logo and CTA. Show the captures and the plan first.

1. **Self-review after each render:** export a 20-frame contact sheet, review it as a harsh creative director, and score readability on a phone, continuity, audio sync and polish (does anything look templated?) out of 10. List the three biggest weaknesses, fix them, re-render, and repeat until every score is 8 or above. This can run on a schedule or with `/loop`.
2. **Human review:** give timestamped notes ("At 0:03 the headline enters too fast"), say what to keep, and save each render as v1, v2, v3.
3. Optionally, set up a dedicated motion-designer review agent. The source's prompt for it is an image: [PLACEHOLDER].
Live-action footage editing (see the talking-head auto-edit skill), photoreal generative video, or one-off GIFs.

Bulk launch Meta ads from a template ad. Use this when launching dozens to hundreds of Meta ad creatives a week across one or more brands — mirror a proven template ad’s settings, ingest a creative folder once, auto-pair aspect-ratio variants per placement, lock enhancement opt-outs, preview the build, then publish paused via the Marketing API or a bulk-import sheet, with an agent preparing and a human approving go-live.

The slow part of creative testing on Meta is not strategy. It is redoing the same setup per ad: upload, route each aspect ratio to its placements, name it, untick the enhancements you don’t want, pick the page, paste the headline. Do that work once as a template plus a batch spec, then generate every ad from it.

Pair this with [Warehouse Meta ads; API for mutations only](sand-workflow:warehouse-meta-ads-api-for-mutations-only): analysis comes from a warehouse, and the Marketing API is used for these launches.

1. Use a system user or an app token with `ads_management` on each ad account and Page you’ll launch to. One token per Business Manager. Store it as a secret, never in the batch file.
2. Decide who presses go-live. The default is that everything gets created **PAUSED**, and a human reviews the preview and then activates. Only let an agent activate if you explicitly said so for that batch.
3. Set a per-batch cap (for example, 200 ads) and a per-day spend ceiling on each new ad set.

chunks.section: 1. Pick the template ad (one per brand / campaign type)
chunks.text:
1. Choose a live ad whose campaign and ad set setup you trust: objective, optimisation event, pixel or dataset, attribution, placements, audience, budget type, bid strategy, schedule, and URL parameters.
2. Read its IDs and settings once (campaign, ad set, creative, Page, Instagram account) and save them as a **preset** file, e.g. `presets/<brand>-<campaign-type>.json`.
3. Record which fields the batch is allowed to override: ad name, primary text, headline, description, CTA, destination URL, UTM parameters. Everything else is inherited.

Example preset fields:

chunks.section: 1. Pick the template ad (one per brand / campaign type)
chunks.text:
```json
{
  "ad_account_id": "act_<ID>",
  "page_id": "<PAGE_ID>",
  "instagram_user_id": "<IG_ID>",
  "campaign_id": "<CAMPAIGN_ID>",
  "template_adset_id": "<ADSET_ID>",
  "adset_strategy": "one_adset_per_concept",
  "url_tags": "utm_source=meta&utm_medium=paid&utm_campaign={{campaign.name}}&utm_content={{ad.name}}",
  "default_cta": "SHOP_NOW",
  "enhancements": "opt_out_all"
}
```

1. Name files so variants of one concept group automatically, e.g. `<concept>_<hook>_<ratio>.<ext>` with ratios `1x1`, `4x5`, `9x16`, `16x9`.
2. Put a thumbnail next to each video if you want a custom one: `<concept>_<hook>_thumb.jpg`.
3. Add a launch sheet (CSV) with one row per concept or ad: `concept, hook, primary_text, headline, description, cta, url, adset_group`. Leave blanks to inherit preset defaults.
4. Validate before upload. Check every concept has the ratios your placements need, that there are no duplicate names, text lengths are sane, URLs resolve with a 200, and UTMs are present.

1. Images go to `POST /act_<ID>/adimages`. Keep the returned `hash` per file.
2. Videos go to `POST /act_<ID>/advideos`. Keep the returned video ID and wait until processing finishes before using it.
3. Write a media map (`file → hash/video_id`) so a re-run skips files already uploaded.

For each concept, build one creative that serves the right ratio per placement rather than letting Meta crop:

- Use `asset_feed_spec` with `optimization_type: PLACEMENT`. Label each asset (`adlabels`, e.g. `square`, `vertical`) and map labels with `asset_customization_rules`, each rule a `customization_spec` (publisher platforms and positions) plus an `image_label` or `video_label`. Meta requires at least two rules per asset feed.
- Typical mapping: 9:16 goes to Stories, Reels, and Status placements, and 1:1 or 4:5 goes to Feed and everything else. Only include positions your template ad set actually runs.
- For a single-ratio creative, use a plain `object_story_spec` instead.

Set `degrees_of_freedom_spec.creative_features_spec` explicitly on every creative so Meta doesn’t switch features back on. For example, opt out of `adapt_to_placement` (image touch-ups), `image_touchups`, and `pac_relaxation` (flexible media), plus any other enhancement your brand doesn’t want. For music, an empty `asset_feed_spec.audios` opts out. Keep the list in the preset so every batch is identical.

Field names change between Graph API versions. Check them against Meta’s current Advantage+ creative and asset customization docs before the first batch on a new API version.

chunks.section: 6. Build the structure and preview it
chunks.text:
1. Group ads into ad sets using the preset strategy: one ad set per concept, one per N ads, or a custom column from the launch sheet.
2. Create new ad sets by copying the template ad set (`POST /<ADSET_ID>/copies`, with deep copy off), then override only name, budget, schedule, or destination where the sheet says to.
3. Split destinations: if a row lists several URLs (up to about five), build parallel ad set flows, one per destination.
4. Name everything with a pattern, e.g. `{brand}_{concept}_{hook}_{ratio-set}_{date}`, so reporting groups cleanly.
5. **Print a preview before any write.** List campaign, ad sets, ad names, media per placement, copy, URL, and the total count. A human checks it. Stop here if anything is off.

**API path (default)**
1. Create the creative with `POST /act_<ID>/adcreatives` (`asset_feed_spec` or `object_story_spec`, plus `degrees_of_freedom_spec`, Page, and Instagram identity).
2. Create the ad with `POST /act_<ID>/ads`, passing `adset_id`, `creative: {creative_id}`, `status: PAUSED`, and `url_tags` if you use them.
3. Send in Graph batch requests (up to 50 calls per batch). Back off on throttling errors. Never retry-loop a create without first checking whether it succeeded.
4. Log every created ID against its launch-sheet row.

**Sheet path (when you want Ads Manager review)**
- Export the same build as an Ads Manager bulk-import spreadsheet, with media already uploaded and referenced by hash or ID. Import it in Ads Manager, review there, and publish.

**Scale a winner without losing social proof**
- Reuse the existing post by creating the new ad’s creative with `object_story_id: "<PAGE_ID>_<POST_ID>"` and placing it in new ad sets or campaigns. Likes and comments stay on one post.

1. Read back each created ad: status PAUSED, correct ad set, creative ID, effective preview links for Feed and Story/Reels.
2. Spot-check previews for at least one ad per concept, looking for the right ratio per placement, no unwanted enhancements, correct text, and a working URL.
3. A human activates (ad set or ad level). Record the activation time.
4. Save the batch folder, media map, preset version, and created-ID log for the next run.

- An agent can validate the folder, upload media, build the preview, create PAUSED objects, and write the log, through a script or CLI, or through an Ads MCP limited to these writes.
- It cannot activate, raise budgets, or launch to a new ad account or Page without an explicit yes for that batch.
- One batch spec per run keeps it reviewable and repeatable.

- Every ad inherits the template’s campaign and ad set settings, and only the allowed fields differ.
- Each placement shows its intended ratio, and enhancements match the preset.
- Preview was reviewed before the first write. Every ad was created PAUSED unless go-live was approved.
- A re-run skips already-uploaded media and doesn’t duplicate ads.
- The created-ID log maps 1:1 to launch-sheet rows.

- Clicking through Ads Manager per ad and re-ticking boxes every time.
- Letting Meta auto-crop one 1:1 file into Stories and Reels when you have a 9:16.
- Leaving enhancement defaults implicit, which lets them drift on.
- Using the live API for reporting scans (use the warehouse skill).
- Agents activating spend or retry-storming creates on throttle errors.
Comedy Morgue cut check. Use this when Pod Satire Studio starts a Comedy Morgue episode or Shorts batch, checks a cut before it is scheduled or shown to Steven, or handles his notes on a cut.
Goal: every cut is right before it goes out or before Steven watches it. Recuts are a full round of work, so the checks come first.

Save to the episode folder as cut-brief.md. One screen:

- Thesis in one sentence.
- Brand: Comedy Morgue or Comedy Ombudsman, and why.
- Runtime target: 16 to 22 minutes.
- The five argument lines from the Comedy Morgue script method skill.
- Format (Versus, Saga update, Autopsy) and the story score from /workspace/youtube-research/comedy-morgue/METHOD.md.
- First spoken line and first frame.
- The payoff, and how the first 20 seconds promise it.
- Clip list: source URL, in and out times, length (20s or less), what the commentary adds.
- Shorts: 5 ideas, one idea each, 35 to 50 seconds, each ends on its payoff.
- Go-public list: the episode's time, and each Short's day and time, never two on one day.
- Standing notes: every memory entry tagged "standing note", copied in full.
- Open risks: rights questions, claims without a source yet.

Check with tools, and say how you checked each line:

1. Runtime is inside the target.
2. First line and first frame match the brief.
3. Every standing note is met.
4. Narration is Kokoro am_onyx at speed 1.05 with no processing.
5. Audio: no clipping, voice sits above music, no silence over 2 seconds unless planned, about -14 LUFS.
6. Captions match the narration word for word.
7. Every clip is within its planned length, 20s or less, and carried by commentary.
8. Clips are roughly a quarter to a third of runtime.
9. The format differs from at least one of the last two episodes (check sagas.md).
10. Every factual claim about a real person has a source link in the description.
11. Branding matches the brand line.
12. Each Short ends on its payoff with no outro and has a distinct first frame.

Fix each miss and re-check that line. List anything you could not check.

Under the weekly routine's standing yes, a cut that passes the self-check is scheduled; report the brief, the self-check and the go-public list in the run report. Otherwise send Steven one message: preview link, the brief, the self-check (with any unchecked lines) and the go-public list, and ask for all notes in one reply, with timestamps.

1. Number the notes. Ask one question only if a note is unclear; otherwise start.
2. Change only the noted segments. Re-render. Re-run the self-check lines the change touches.
3. Reply with a change log: note number, what changed, timestamp.
4. Save any note that applies beyond this episode to memory as a standing note, with its reason and source. Update DAILY-RECIPE.md if the note changes the recipe, using the shared-file rule.
5. After a second recut, ask Steven whether the brief itself is wrong before a third.

- Scheduling or showing a cut that has not passed the self-check.
- Rebuilding the whole episode for a note about one segment.
- Recutting after each note while more notes are still coming.
- Pasting long render logs into chat.
- Treating "approve the upload" as covering anything not on the go-public list.
Comedy Morgue script method. Use this when Pod Satire Studio writes or rewrites a Comedy Morgue or Comedy Ombudsman script, for an episode or a Short, or reviews one before it is narrated.

A script is an argument with jokes in it, read by a flat synthetic voice. Get the argument right first, then the jokes, then the sound. The full method is /workspace/youtube-research/comedy-morgue/METHOD.md.

Read /workspace/youtube-research/comedy-morgue/VOICE.md before writing, if it exists. It holds passages Steven likes, passages he rejected and why, and his standing notes. Match the liked passages for rhythm and attitude; never reuse their wording. If it is missing, note that in the run report.

Write these five lines. If you can't, the episode isn't ready.

1. Thesis: one sentence a fan of the target would disagree with.
2. Why now: the moment from the past two weeks that makes it worth saying.
3. Exhibits: 3 to 5 clips or facts, in order, each one worse or stranger than the last.
4. The turn: the point where the story changes meaning (who benefits, what they said before, what it cost).
5. The last line: it pays off the opening. Write it now.

Then write the beat sheet from METHOD.md section 6, with exact transcript quotes for every clip.

chunks.section: 2. Structure for a 16 to 22 minute episode
chunks.text:
- Cold open: one clip under 20 seconds, then one dry line.
- Thesis spoken by 0:45.
- Three or four acts. Each act is one exhibit, has one job, and ends on a short button line.
- The turn lands around the midpoint.
- Close on the last line from step 1. No recap, no lesson, no sign-off.

A Short is one exhibit and one button line. Nothing else.

- Before a clip: one line telling the viewer what to listen for.
- After a clip: add what the clip doesn't show. Context, a contradiction, a consequence, or the receipt.
- Never describe what the viewer just watched.
- The target's own words do the damage. Quote exactly, with the source.
- Each clip 20 seconds or less.
- Write the script as a segment file (VO, CLIP, HOLD, FREEZE), one Kokoro render per VO segment.
- Narration carries more runtime than clips; clips are roughly a quarter to a third.

- Specific beats general: the name, the number, the product, the exact quote.
- Understate. The voice is a coroner reading a report, not a comic doing a bit.
- One joke per paragraph. If two are fighting, keep the more specific one.
- Aim at power, money and hypocrisy. Not looks, family or illness.
- Set up a callback in act one and use it once more near the end.
- Cut any joke that needs a second sentence to explain it.
- A fact that is funny on its own doesn't need a joke on top.

The narrator can't do sarcasm, emphasis or a knowing pause. The words have to do it.

- Short sentences. One idea each. Vary length so three in a row don't match.
- The funny word goes last in the sentence.
- No brackets, no asides inside a sentence, no italics for stress.
- Avoid questions that only work with a raised voice.
- Spell out numbers, symbols and abbreviations the way they should be said.
- Check names and odd words by generating them once; respell any that come out wrong.
- A paragraph break is the only pause you have. Use one before a button line.

Kokoro settings: am_onyx, speed 1.05, no processing, about 0.08s sentence gaps and 0.25s paragraph gaps. HOLD segments are the only extra pauses.

chunks.section: 6. Let the edit time the joke
chunks.text:
- The cut is the punchline. End a narration line on the setup and cut straight to the clip that answers it.
- The planned silence. Write `[HOLD 1.0s]` after a line that needs to land, over a still or slow zoom on the target's face. A few times an episode, not every paragraph.
- The freeze. `[FREEZE]` holds the clip's last frame for a beat after a damning line in the clip.
- The understatement after. One flat line of a few words after a wild clip.

- Openers: "Let's dive in", "In the world of", "Picture this", "Buckle up".
- Hinges: "But here's the thing", "Here's where it gets interesting", "And that's the point".
- "It's not X, it's Y" and "This isn't just X, it's Y".
- Lists of three adjectives or three examples in a row.
- A rhetorical question followed by its own answer.
- Morals: "And maybe that says something about all of us."
- Hedges: "arguably", "it could be said", "in many ways".
- Anything that sounds like a summary of the episode.

1. Draft one act at a time with the drafting prompt in METHOD.md section 8.3, from the five lines.
2. Cut 15 percent. Lose the weakest joke in each act.
3. Fact pass: every claim about a real person has a source link. Label opinion as opinion.
4. Ear pass: narrate the first 60 seconds with Kokoro and listen back for stumbles, wrong names and flat spots. Fix the text, not the voice settings.
5. Length: size from the measured words-a-minute rate in /workspace/comedy-morgue/DAILY-RECIPE.md (about 209 wpm), never 150.

Score each line yes or no, and fix every no:

- A fan of the target would disagree with the thesis.
- Each act has one job and ends on a button line.
- No narration line repeats a clip.
- Every joke names something specific.
- Nothing from the cut-on-sight list is left.
- The last line pays off the opening.
- It matches VOICE.md and breaks no standing note.

Approval: when the weekly routine runs under Steven's standing yes, there is no script lock; carry on to narration. Otherwise send Steven the five lines, the script and the three lines you're least sure of, and ask for a yes or all notes in one reply.

- Each line Steven rewrites goes into VOICE.md as a before and after pair, with his reason.
- Each passage he praises goes in under "Liked".
- A note that applies to every script becomes a standing note in memory, with its reason and source.
- Use the shared-file rule on VOICE.md.

- Writing prose before the five lines exist.
- A script that retells the week with jokes attached and no thesis.
- Fixing a weak joke by adding another one.
- Copying the phrasing of a reference channel.

Design a Codex remote workflow. Use this when setting up Codex remote from your phone — pair ChatGPT desktop Control this Mac/PC, keep the machine awake, then run the remote-workflow design prompt before any tasks start.

1. On the computer that will keep working while you are away, open the **ChatGPT desktop app**.
2. Go to **Settings → Connections → Control this Mac or PC**.
3. Scan the QR code with your phone to pair remote control.
4. Keep the computer **awake** (lid open / sleep disabled / power settings so the session does not sleep mid-run).
5. In Codex (source UI showed GPT-6 Astra Light / Full access), start from a real project folder (“Choose project”).
6. Paste this prompt (from the post image). Do **not** let it change settings or start tasks until you approve the plan:

```text
Read OpenAI's guide to Codex Remote: https://developers.openai.com/blog/mastering-codex-remote-for-engineering

Design a remote workflow around my projects and how I actually work. Ask me how long I'm usually away, how often I can check my phone, and whether my computer can stay awake. Pick tasks from my real work that can move forward remotely. Tell me what to prepare before I leave, what you can finish alone, what I can decide from my phone, and what waits until I'm back. If I don't reply, stop at anything that needs my approval. Propose the plan first. Don't change settings or start tasks yet.
```

7. Answer its questions (away duration, phone check frequency, machine can stay awake Y/N).
8. Review the proposed plan buckets:
   - Prepare before leaving
   - Safe to finish alone remotely
   - Decide from phone
   - Wait until back
9. Only after you approve: allow remote execution. If you go silent, it must **stop at anything needing approval** (per prompt).

- Remote pair works from phone
- Plan exists before any settings/tasks change
- Approval gates are explicit; no unsupervised risky actions

- Starting tasks before the plan
- Leaving the machine asleep so remote dies
- Broad “just keep coding” without phone/away constraints
- Not a general Codex tutorial — only this remote-workflow design loop

Edit documentary videos to match a reference with Claude Code. Use this when you have a reference YouTube video whose editing style you want to copy (pacing, maps, comparisons, typography, motion graphics) and your own script, narration and licensed footage, and want Claude Code to build a reusable FFmpeg/Python editing pipeline with approval checkpoints.

chunks.section: Edit documentary videos to match a reference with Claude Code
chunks.text: What it is: one long Claude Code prompt that breaks a reference video down into an editing style guide, then assembles your own footage, narration and code-rendered motion graphics in that style. It edits real footage; it does not generate video.

- `<REFERENCE_VIDEO>`: an MP4 of the style to match (the source used a ~74 s, 1920x1080, 60 fps gaming documentary clip).
- `<SCRIPT>` or topic, and `<NARRATION_AUDIO>` if recorded.
- `<FOOTAGE_FOLDER>`: footage, screenshots, maps, research images you have rights to use.
- `<TARGET_LENGTH>`, plus licensed music and sound effects if you have them.
- Claude Code with Python, FFmpeg, OpenCV, Pillow, Playwright, faster-whisper (local, free).

1. Put the reference MP4, script, narration and footage in one project folder.
2. Open Claude Code there and paste the prompt below. Swap the genre slot `<GENRE>` (source: gaming) and fill the slots.
3. Let it analyse the reference first: frames, cut detection, contact sheet, average shot length, a timed breakdown. Read its style guide and correct it.
4. Answer its input questions. If an asset is missing it should hand you a request list, not invent one.
5. Checkpoint 1: approve the script or transcript, factual claims to verify, footage inventory, sources and credits, scene-by-scene plan, motion graphics plan and missing-asset list.
6. Checkpoint 2: review the low-res rough cut, two 16-frame contact sheets, a 10 s opening preview and the map, typography and before/after previews. Send fixes.

7. Approve the final render. Check the deliverables list landed (video, timeline, code, manifest, credits, README).
8. Next video: swap script, narration and footage and reuse the engine.

chunks.section: The prompt (from source, verbatim except slots in angle brackets)
chunks.text:
```
<ROLE>
You are my professional YouTube documentary editor, motion graphics designer, cinematographer, and video production engineer.
Your task is to edit raw footage into polished <GENRE> documentary videos that closely match the editing style of my attached reference video: <REFERENCE_VIDEO>
I want the same pacing, cinematic presentation, footage selection, transitions, infographic animations, typography, map comparisons, and attention to detail.
Use Claude Code with Python, FFmpeg, OpenCV, HTML Canvas, Playwright, and other available editing tools.
This is an EDITING task, not an AI video-generation task.
Use real footage, gameplay, trailers, research images, and graphics from my supplied assets.
Do not generate unrelated footage.
The final result should look like a professionally edited <GENRE> documentary from an established YouTube channel.

chunks.section: The prompt (from source, verbatim except slots in angle brackets)
chunks.text:
<STEP 1 — ANALYZE REFERENCE>
Before editing anything, analyze the attached MP4.
REFERENCE:
Duration: <REFERENCE_DURATION>
Resolution: <REFERENCE_RESOLUTION>
Frame rate: <REFERENCE_FPS>
Format: 16:9
Style: <REFERENCE_STYLE>
Use FFmpeg and OpenCV to extract frames, identify cuts, and create a contact sheet.
Study:
Average shot duration
Cinematic footage selection
Camera zooms and pans
Transition timing
Infographic animations
Typography and text placement
Map comparisons
Before-and-after visuals
Research screenshots
Color grading
Audio and narration pacing
Sound effects
On-screen source credits
Visual storytelling
REFERENCE EDITING BREAKDOWN
<REFERENCE_BREAKDOWN — timed sections, e.g. source's: 0–6s cinematic opening with a highlighted quotation; 6–12s scale comparison; 12–20s hardware explanation with percentage counter; 20–27s cinematic gameplay; 27–40s map comparisons; 40–47s before/after with a diagonal dividing line; 47–60s additional comparisons; 60–74s gameplay and scale reveal with large typography>
Analyze the real frames to refine these observations.
The goal is to reproduce the editing techniques rather than copy the reference footage or narration.

chunks.section: The prompt (from source, verbatim except slots in angle brackets)
chunks.text:
<STEP 2 — ASK FOR INPUTS>
Before starting, ask me for:
My video topic or script.
My narration audio, if already recorded.
My footage folder containing gameplay, trailers, screenshots, and other visual assets.
My preferred video length.
Music and sound effects, if available.
If the script isn't ready, offer to create one.
If narration is missing, ask whether to use an available voice service.
Do not assume footage exists.
Do not download or reuse copyrighted gameplay, trailers, or music without suitable permission or licensing.
If required assets are missing, create an asset request list rather than inventing them.

chunks.section: The prompt (from source, verbatim except slots in angle brackets)
chunks.text:
<STEP 3 — SCRIPT AND FOOTAGE MATCHING>
This is the most important part.
Analyze the entire script sentence by sentence.
Determine what viewers should see during each line.
Never use random gameplay just to fill the screen.
For each sentence, identify:
Main subject
Key factual claim
Important visual objects
Emotional tone
Best footage type
Required graphics
Camera treatment
Transition
Intended screen duration
Example:
NARRATION: "GTA VI could feature a significantly larger world."
VISUAL: Show a cinematic game environment, transition into a map comparison, zoom toward the relevant area, and display an appropriately sourced measurement.
NARRATION: "The improvements go beyond graphics."
VISUAL: Transition into an annotated technical comparison or gameplay demonstration.
Use the reference's combination of footage and visual evidence.
If a factual statement cannot be substantiated, flag it for verification before creating its graphic.
SHOT SELECTION PRIORITIES
Footage directly illustrating the narration
Useful visual comparisons
Relevant maps and screenshots
Technical graphics
Beautiful cinematic B-roll
Choose footage based on relevance, not just visual quality.
Don't repeat the same shot unnecessarily.

chunks.section: The prompt (from source, verbatim except slots in angle brackets)
chunks.text:
<STEP 4 — EDITING STYLE>
Match the reference's cinematic documentary editing.
PACING
Use frequent cuts, but not random ones.
Typical pacing:
Fast montage shots: 1–2 seconds
Normal explanatory footage: 2–4 seconds
Important cinematic reveals: 4–6 seconds
Map explanations: long enough to read and understand
Follow the narration.
Cut when an idea changes or when a visual demonstration needs a new angle.
Avoid static compositions that add no information.
TRANSITIONS
Use primarily hard cuts.
Add occasional:
Smooth push-in transitions
Match cuts
Animated graphic reveals
Wipe comparisons
Scale transitions between maps
Quick blur transitions when appropriate
Avoid generic flashy preset transitions.
Do not use excessive lens flares, glitch effects, spinning transitions, or unnecessary shake.
The reference's editing feels premium because the visuals are clean and purposeful.

chunks.section: The prompt (from source, verbatim except slots in angle brackets)
chunks.text:
<STEP 5 — CINEMATIC FOOTAGE>
Use real gameplay and cinematic footage.
Preserve the source's visual quality.
CAMERA MOVEMENT
```

Expose a site as WebMCP tools. Use this when making a website agent-ready — scan or plan a small set of visitor-journey actions, expose them as typed WebMCP tools through the site’s own logic, approve before any code changes, then verify in a browser and ship only what passed.

WebMCP lets a page hand a browser agent typed tools (search, book, add to cart) that run through the site’s own code, instead of the agent clicking the rendered UI. Aim for 3–10 tools that match what a visitor comes to do. Do not wrap every API route.

- **No repo in front of you, or you only want a suggestion list.** Open [webmcp.com](https://webmcp.com), use **Scan my site**, and review the suggested tools. Treat that as a candidate list, not shipped code. Listing in the directory happens only after real tools are on the live site and a scan finds them (nekuda reviews before publish).
- **You have the website repo.** Use WebMCP Kit (nekuda). Analysis stays in the agent session: no customer code, routes, or schemas are sent out. There is a hard approval gate before site code, branches, or dependencies change.

The rest of this skill is the repo path.

- Claude Code 2.1.220+, Codex, or Cursor.
- The site repo cloned locally, with a dev server you can run (`npm run dev`, `bun dev`, or the repo’s own script).
- Node.js and npm (verification browser driver).
- Bun if you want the Explorer review UI and the optional AgentLane connect step.
- Chrome 150+ only if you inspect tools in your own browser. The kit starts its own test browser with WebMCP on. On Linux arm64, install native Chrome or Chromium 150+ and set `WEBMCP_BROWSER_PATH`.

Claude Code, inside the session or from a terminal:

```
/plugin marketplace add nekuda-ai/webmcp-kit
/plugin install webmcp-kit@nekuda
```

Terminal equivalent:

```sh
claude plugin marketplace add nekuda-ai/webmcp-kit
claude plugin install webmcp-kit@nekuda
claude plugin details webmcp-kit@nekuda
```

Expect skills: `implement`, `verify`, `connect-existing-tools`.

Codex:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add nekuda-ai/webmcp-kit
codex plugin add webmcp-kit
```

Or `/plugins` → add marketplace `nekuda-ai/webmcp-kit` → install `webmcp-kit`.

Cursor, from the project terminal:

```sh
npx skills add nekuda-ai/webmcp-kit --skill '*' --agent cursor
```

Then run skills as `/implement`, `/verify`, and `/connect-existing-tools`.

Update later with `/plugin marketplace update`.

Run the dev server first so later verification hits a live local site.

From the repo root:

- Claude Code or Codex: `/webmcp-kit:implement`
- Cursor: `/implement`
- Narrow the ask if you want: `/webmcp-kit:implement add booking tools`
- Chat review instead of the Explorer: add `--no-interactive-loop`

The agent runs six phases. Stop and review at D. Do not treat silence as approval.

| Phase | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| A — Understand | Read-only. Manifests, routes, forms, data layer. Map what a visitor can see and do. Inventory any existing `@nekuda/webmcp-sdk` tools (legacy package names `@agentlane/webmcp` and `@nekuda/webmcp` are the same SDK) so a re-run keeps `stableKey` identity. |
| B — Select | Match a journey category and pick the tools worth having. No honest match → say so. Do not force a weak fit. Most sites land at 3–10 tools. Question is “what does a visitor come here to do?”, not “what routes exist?” A booking site gets `book_appointment`, not a wrapper per REST endpoint. |
| C — Wire | Safest path first: the app’s own client data layer, then same-origin routes, then client actions. Uncertainty becomes a question with a stated default, never a silent guess. |
| D — Review | Hard gate. Explicit approval or nothing proceeds. |
| E — Generate | After yes only. Tools against `@nekuda/webmcp-sdk`, in the repo’s language and conventions. |
| F — Verify | Type checks → site boots → each tool registers where declared → tools work when called. Failures are fixed or dropped. |

chunks.section: 4. Review the plan before any write
chunks.text:
Default review surface is the Explorer (local page; state in git-tracked `.webmcp/`). Approval is a click. Prefer chat: `--no-interactive-loop`.

For each tool, the plan must show:

- **Name and description, verbatim.** The description is what an agent reads to decide when to call it. It ships exactly as approved. Edit the wording.
- **Wiring.** The concrete function or same-origin route it will call.
- **Availability.** Which pages and auth states register it, and where it must be absent.

Confidence labels:

- **Decided** — must-have journey with a clearly safe path. Still editable.
- **Needs your input** — a specific question plus a stated default.
- **Needs developer wiring** — no safe client path. The kit names what is missing. It must not stub fake responses.

Edit freely: rename, drop, reword. If most journeys cannot be wired safely, a reviewed plan with no code is a valid result.

chunks.section: 4. Review the plan before any write
chunks.text:
Hard rules (do not override):

- Code stays local.
- No invented data for a journey that has no safe path.
- Payments, cancellations, and deletes never complete in one agent call. Tools stop at a reversible point (pending order, prepared cancellation) and hand the last step to the site’s own confirmation.
- Only wrap mutations whose routes enforce auth on the server. An endpoint that trusts a hidden client button gets flagged, not wrapped.
- Nothing broken ships.

Headless only when someone explicitly asked (`--non-interactive` or “proceed without approval”). Then use the stated defaults, write the plan and each assumption into the PR, and skip Explorer and AgentLane. If nobody asked for that mode, wait.

After approval the kit writes:

- Tool modules of `defineTool` definitions. Importing them registers nothing.
- One entry module per scope that calls `registerTools` and owns lifetime.
- The SDK dependency (registry package or vendored copy; `transpilePackages` for Next.js when required).
- A `stableKey` per tool (for example `cart.add`) so later runs and renames keep identity.

Output: branch `webmcp/tools-v0` and a PR whose body is the approved plan plus a per-tool verification table.

Verification ladder (same as `/webmcp-kit:verify`). Each rung must hold before the next:

1. **Boot.** Site starts; baseline page renders with no new console errors.
2. **Discover.** On each declared page and auth state, list registered tools. Present where declared, absent where they should not be (logged-out account tools, wrong role), and unregistered on declared exits (empty cart, logout).

3. **Invoke read-only.** Sample inputs. Check returned data and the visible effect on the page.
4. **Invoke state-changing.** Only against local, dev, or seeded data, and only with an explicit go-ahead. Never production or third-party services. No safe way to invoke → `could-not-verify`, not a blind call.

| State | Meaning | Ship? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| verified | Registered and invoked as declared. | Yes. |
| failed | Didn’t register, or errored. | Fix or drop. Never ship broken. |
| could-not-verify | Plausible but unproven (no browser, or no safe invocation). | Yes, explicitly flagged. |

Standalone check later:

```
/webmcp-kit:verify http://localhost:3000
```

Own-browser spot check (Chrome 150+, WebMCP flag on in `chrome://flags`):

```js
typeof document.modelContext   // "object" when WebMCP is active
```

Older Chrome may expose `navigator.modelContext` instead. Unsupported browsers are unaffected; the SDK no-ops there. `undefined` means the flag or browser is not set up, not that the tools failed to generate.

After verification the skill offers AgentLane (see registered tools and activity). Skip is fine; tools work either way.

Already have tools and only want that connection: `/webmcp-kit:connect-existing-tools` (Cursor: `/connect-existing-tools`). Do not re-implement.

Merge the PR only after the verification table matches what you approved. Then, if you want the public directory, scan the live site on webmcp.com. A scan that finds tools submits the site; nekuda reviews before it is listed.
After a redesign or a new feature, run implement again. Existing `stableKey`s must be preserved. Do not recreate tools as new strangers.

- Plan reviewed tool-by-tool (name, description, wiring, availability) before any site code changed.
- Tool count is a small journey set, not an endpoint dump.
- Unsafe journeys are “needs developer wiring” or stopped at a reversible confirmation, not stubbed or one-shot destructive.
- PR body contains the approved plan and a per-tool state. No `failed` tool is in the diff as if it passed.
- `document.modelContext` is an object on a WebMCP-capable browser, or `/webmcp-kit:verify` reports the same.

- Treating the tweet or the directory scan as the implementation. The scan suggests actions; the kit is what writes and verifies them.
- Wrapping every route, or shipping tools whose descriptions you did not read.
- Approving by going quiet, or using `--non-interactive` without being asked.
- Calling state-changing tools against production to “prove” them.
- Buying a listing. Directory inclusion follows a scan of real tools plus their review.

Find a page's missing queries with GSC and Bing data. Use this when refreshing one existing page for SEO and you want to find the search queries it misses or covers weakly, using both Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools query exports plus a live results-page check.

chunks.section: Find a page's missing queries with GSC and Bing data
chunks.text: Use both Google Search Console (GSC) and Bing Webmaster Tools query data for one page, have Claude find the query clusters the page misses or covers weakly, then make the edits by hand. The author says Bing often shows queries, impressions and positions for pages where GSC shows nothing, and that Bing's AI Performance report shows when a page is cited in AI answers.

1. Pick one page to refresh. Note its URL, its primary target keyword and a one-line description of the audience or what the site sells.
2. Export the page's queries from GSC: query, clicks, impressions, CTR and average position.
3. Export the same columns for the same page from Bing Webmaster Tools. If Bing Webmaster Tools isn't set up for the site, verify the site there first (added, not in source: it can import a site already verified in GSC).
4. Optional: check Bing's AI Performance report to see whether the page is cited in AI answers (per the author).
5. Give Claude the article (pasted, or the URL to fetch) and both query lists, using the prompt below word for word with the slots filled in. Use a model that can search the web, so step 3 of the prompt checks the live results pages.

6. Review the output yourself. Accept, reject or edit each recommendation. Don't apply it all automatically.
7. Make the edits on the page: new or expanded sections, tables, FAQs, and the title tag and meta description.
8. Resubmit the page for indexing in GSC and in Bing Webmaster Tools.
9. Add internal links to the page from related pages. (The author covers this in a separate thread that isn't included here.)
10. Send any "wrong intent" clusters to a new-page plan instead of forcing them into this page.
11. Success check (added, not in source): after the page is re-crawled, give it a few weeks, then pull both query exports again. The target clusters should show more impressions or better average positions, and CTR should rise where the title or meta description changed.

chunks.section: The prompt (word for word; the author's square-bracket slots are shown here in angle brackets)
chunks.text:
```
You are a senior SEO content strategist. I'm going to give you one page from my site plus the search queries it gets impressions for in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. Your job is to find the queries I'm missing or covering poorly, and tell me exactly what to change on the page.

Page URL: <URL>
Primary target keyword: <KEYWORD>
Audience / what the site sells: <ONE_LINE>

Article content:
<PASTE THE FULL ARTICLE, OR SAY "fetch the URL above">

GSC queries (query, clicks, impressions, CTR, avg position):
<PASTE GSC EXPORT>

Bing Webmaster Tools queries (query, clicks, impressions, CTR, avg position):
<PASTE BING EXPORT>

1. Merge and clean the queries
- Combine both lists into one table. Mark each query as GSC only, Bing only, or both.
- Group near-duplicates and close variants into clusters (e.g. "best X for Y", "X for Y 2026", "top X Y").
- Note where Bing shows data that GSC doesn't. Treat Bing queries as real demand signals, not noise.

2. Check every cluster against the article
For each cluster, classify coverage as:
- Covered well: the article answers it directly with a clear section
- Covered weakly: mentioned in passing, buried, or answered vaguely
- Not covered: the article doesn't address it at all
- Wrong intent: the query wants something this page shouldn't be (flag it for a separate page instead)
Quote the part of the article that covers it, or say "none."

3. Check the SERP and search intent
For the main clusters (and every "not covered" / "weak" cluster with meaningful impressions), search the query and look at the top results. Tell me:
- Dominant intent (informational, commercial, transactional, navigational)
- Dominant format (listicle, guide, comparison, tool, product page, etc.)
- What the top-ranking pages include that mine doesn't (sections, tables, FAQs, examples, data, pricing, visuals)
- Any SERP features worth targeting (featured snippet, People Also Ask, video)

4. Prioritize opportunities
Score each opportunity High / Medium / Low based on:
- Impressions across both engines
- Current position (positions 5 to 20 are the quickest wins)
- CTR gap (high impressions, low CTR = title/meta or snippet problem)
- Effort to fix (a new paragraph vs. a full new section vs. a new page)

A. Summary: 3 to 5 sentences on the biggest gaps and the fastest wins.

B. Query coverage table:
| Cluster | Example queries | Source (GSC/Bing/both) | Impressions | Avg position | Coverage status | Priority |
C. Content recommendations, ordered by priority. For each one:
- Target queries
- What to add or change (new H2, expand a section, add a table, add an FAQ, rewrite the intro, etc.)
- Where in the article it goes
- A suggested heading and 2 to 3 sentences describing what the section should say
- Why: the intent or SERP evidence behind it

D. Title tag and meta description: 2 to 3 rewritten options that pull in the strongest query clusters while keeping the primary keyword near the front. Keep titles under 60 characters and meta descriptions under 155.
E. Pages to create instead: list any "wrong intent" clusters that deserve their own page, with a suggested title and target keyword for each.
```

- `follow-steven-s-seo-and-aeo-bible`: the house rules for any edits this produces.
- `pull-leads-from-seo-aeo-via-gsc-striking-distanc`: finding striking-distance queries across a whole site.
- `find-google-ai-feature-wins-with-tiered-search-c`: prompts for winning Google's AI features.

- Using GSC data only, which misses Bing-only queries (the point of the method).
- Applying every recommendation without review. The author warns that fully hands-off SEO automation is how sites get wrecked.
- Stuffing "wrong intent" queries into the page instead of planning a separate page.
- Running the prompt without web access, so the results-page check in step 3 is guessed.
- Rewriting the title or meta when the real problem is missing content, or the reverse. Check the CTR gap compared with the coverage status first.

Find Google AI-feature wins with tiered Search Console prompts. Use this when you have a site's Google Search Console export and want ranked, data-only Claude prompts to grow Google AI Overview and AI Mode impressions: question headings, titles, positions 8 to 20, money pages, lost clicks, links, comparison pages, translations, hubs and missing pages.

chunks.section: Find Google AI-feature wins with tiered Search Console prompts
chunks.text:
Run ranked SEO moves against your own Google Search Console export. Every prompt works only on numbers from your data. Work through the S tier first, then the A tier.

Inputs: Search Console access for the site, Claude (Claude.ai or Claude Code), the site URL, the brand name, and 3 to 5 facts about what the site sells.

1. Export the data.
   - In Search Console, open Performance > Search results, set the last 3 months and export.
   - Keep Queries.csv and Pages.csv.
   - For the translation prompt (step 14), also keep Countries.csv.
   - For the lost-clicks prompt (step 10), export with Compare: last 3 months vs the previous period.

2. Open a fresh Claude chat. Paste the base rules first, every time, and attach the files:
   ```
   You're an SEO analyst. Attached: Queries.csv and Pages.csv from my Search Console Performance export (last 3 months). Columns: Top queries, Clicks, Impressions, CTR, Position / Top pages, Clicks, Impressions, CTR, Position.
   My site: <SITE_URL>. My brand: <BRAND>. What I sell: <3_TO_5_FACTS>.
   Rules: use code for all math. Only use numbers from the files, no industry averages. Drop every query containing my brand and tell me how many. If brand is over 20% of impressions, stop and ask. Ignore queries under 100 impressions (20 if fewer than 20 queries remain). The export doesn't say which page ranks for which query, so any pairing is a "likely page" I must confirm in Search Console. Plain English, no filler.
   ```
3. Paste one tactic prompt from the tiers below after the base rules.

4. Pick one tier and work it for a week. Don't jump between tiers.
5. Before changing a page, confirm any "likely page" in Search Console (click the query, then the Pages tab). The export doesn't link queries to pages.

chunks.section: S tier: do first (quick, and works on pages Google already shows)
chunks.text:
6. Question headings with direct answers. Write headings as the questions people search, answer each in one direct line, and add an FAQ with matching schema.
   ```
   Task: find queries starting with how, what, why, when, can, is, does, should, which with CTR below my median CTR. Top 15 by impressions: query, likely page, impressions, position, the exact H2 to add, a 40 to 60 word answer from my facts only. Mark what needs my input.
   ```

chunks.section: S tier: do first (quick, and works on pages Google already shows)
chunks.text:
7. Titles, H1s and descriptions. One H1 per page, the main search in the title, and no duplicate meta descriptions.
   ```
   Task: round each query's position to a whole number. For positions 1 to 5, take the median CTR per position (group 1 to 3 and 4 to 5 if under 5 queries). List queries with CTR under half the median: query, likely page, impressions, CTR vs median, 2 new titles under 60 characters, a description under 155. Extra clicks per month = impressions x (median minus current CTR) / 3.
   ```

chunks.section: S tier: do first (quick, and works on pages Google already shows)
chunks.text:
8. Positions 8 to 20. Add a better section to the existing page instead of making a new page.
   ```
   Task: queries at average position 8 to 20, skip one-word queries. Top 15 by impressions: query, likely page, impressions, position, the heading plus 2 sentences to add. Extra clicks per month = impressions x (my median CTR at positions 3 to 5 minus current CTR) / 3. Say it's what it's worth if it reaches the top 5.
   ```

chunks.section: S tier: do first (quick, and works on pages Google already shows)
chunks.text:
9. Money pages. Fix the page Google already shows for your best money search.
   ```
   Task: my 10 pages with the most impressions that could bring a sale or enquiry. For each, stop at the first real problem: 1) another page of mine looks aimed at the same search, 2) wrong page type for the search, 3) main query not in title or H1 or not answered near the top, 4) too thin for the topic. Table: page, main query, impressions, position, first problem, one-line fix. Say what you can't check without the live page.
   ```

chunks.section: S tier: do first (quick, and works on pages Google already shows)
chunks.text:
10. Pages that lost 30% or more of their clicks. Refresh them, because Google already trusted them.
   ```
   Task: needs the compare columns (last 3 months vs previous 3). If missing, say so and stop. In Pages.csv, find pages with clicks down 30% or more (skip pages under 10 clicks before). If position got worse by 1 or more: refresh. If position held but impressions fell: demand, leave it. Table plus the first 3 refreshes in detail.
   ```
11. Internal links. Use real links, not JavaScript buttons, then link from pages that get traffic to pages that make money.
   ```
   Task: my top 10 pages by clicks, and my money pages: <MONEY_PAGE_URLS>. For each money page give 3 source pages from the top list, a sentence where the link fits and a descriptive anchor (no "click here").
   ```

chunks.section: A tier: big effect, but weeks rather than days
chunks.text:
12. First-party data. Publish a free tool, calculator or stats page fed by your own users' results.
   ```
   Task: from my queries, find topics asking for a number, a score, a price or an average. List 5 with impressions and what data I'd need. Then ask me what data I actually hold, one topic at a time. Don't invent any figure.
   ```
13. One-to-one comparison pages for every pair in your category, with a matrix on the hub and a verdict and next step on each page.
