- Architecture mentions include Nostr, Postgres, Redis.
- Goose is the related agent runtime Buzz can rely on — not the same as Buzz itself.

- Not a general “how to build an AI business” playbook — only Buzz self-host setup from the source post + README quick start shown in the video
- Do not invent ACL schemas or runtime flags beyond current Buzz docs for your version
- Do not confuse Buzz (workspace/relay) with goose (agent runtime)

Steer creative work away from the default pick. Use this when a creative choice is left to you (names, slogans, hooks, ideas, poster or thumbnail looks, colour, layout, page or app design) or when work reads as generic, safe or 'typical AI'. Not for code, bug fixes or choices already made.

chunks.section: Steer creative work away from the default pick
chunks.text:
Use this whenever a creative choice is left to you: names, slogans, titles, hooks, story or game ideas, poster and thumbnail looks, colour, layout, page or app design. Don't use it for code identifiers, bug fixes, choices Steven has already made, or text whose form a standing rule already sets.

The idea: your first answer is the average of everything that's already been made. It feels right because it's familiar, and that's exactly why it's generic. So name that answer, then move away from it for a reason that only fits this project.

- Steven's standing rules win over this skill: the bot's profile, the Humanise writing rule, the SEO and AEO Bible, and any brand or channel playbook. Use this skill only for what those rules leave open.
- If Steven asks for the plain, standard or expected version, give him that.

1. Find the starting point outside your own taste.
   - If the request has real context (a project, place, person, audience, purpose or limit), start from that.
   - If the request is thin and the job is short (a name, a few slogans, a short text), make the work from a seed or a guess you state openly. Then end with one short question asking for a fact about the case, not for permission to redo it.
   - If the request is thin and the job is long or costly (a full design, a long text, a game system), ask that one question first: who it's for, where it'll live, or what it's about.
   - If the request is thin and Steven wants it now, roll a seed (step 2).
   - Never choose the starting point by asking yourself what would be most interesting, because that question lands every user in the same place.

2. Roll a seed when there's no context. Pick one value from each list at random. Use real randomness, such as Python's `random.choice` on the box; your own pick drifts to the default. Keep any axis the subject already fixes, and reroll a value once if it clashes with the subject.
   - Visual seed. Pick a method, a colour, a layout and a type style.
     - Methods: risograph print, linocut, embroidery, hand-painted shop sign, chalk on pavement, LED dot matrix, old CRT screen, thermal receipt printer, airport departure board, e-ink display, CAD wireframe, flash film photo, x-ray image, thermal camera image, satellite image, security camera still, weather radar map, neon tubes, stained glass, glazed ceramic, clay model photo, folded paper, shadow puppets.

- Colour: one ink only, two colours that clash, colours of the subject's material, very dark and low key, colours of a place at a set hour, grey with one warm spot, the colours of a machine screen.
     - Layout: subject huge and cropped by the edges, subject tiny in a large empty field, seen from straight above, one thing repeated many times, the text is the image, low and off centre, one big shape and nothing else.
     - Type: cut-out letters, stencil, tall condensed, typewriter, one giant word, letters built from the subject, type set vertically.
     - Add a verb (trade, hide, repair, wait, signal) and a scale (one person, a street, a crowd of strangers) and build the idea from who does what.
   - Text seed. Pick a voice, a way in and a register.

- Voice: a witness in first person, a short letter, overheard dialogue, a review by someone tired, someone who disagrees, a rumour passed on.
     - Way in: a sound, a single object, a mistake, a rule, a thing that's missing, a complaint, the ending.
     - Register: plain, dry, blunt, warm, terse, nervous.
   - Idea seed. Pick a verb, a constraint, a scale and a pressure.
     - Constraint: only one try, it gets worse when you wait, someone else controls half of it, the reward is also the cost.
     - Pressure: a deadline, a rival, a debt, a rule that changes, running out of space.
   - Setting and region (optional). Use the everyday detail someone living there would know, not the famous sights, flag colours or national dish. If you don't know real local detail, use less of it.

3. Name the default. Before answering, write one line for yourself: "the default here is X." Don't use X unless the context calls for it.
4. Move away from it using this case. Lean on the project's world, its limits, its audience and its odd details. A good choice could only belong here. Don't swap a cliché for its well-known opposite (dark instead of bright, minimal instead of busy), because that's just the second most common answer. Odd with no reason is as empty as safe.
5. Give one reason per choice. Each choice needs a reason you can say in one sentence, drawn from a fact about this project.
6. For text:
   - If a sentence could be pasted into another project unchanged, rewrite it until it couldn't.
   - Prefer the concrete detail over the general claim, and the plain word over the impressive one.

- Avoid the usual opening, structure and ending, but stay within the length and format Steven set.
   - Cut these:
     - offers to redo the text or notes about the text
     - bold headers or labels nobody asked for
     - bullets where sentences would do
     - a closing call to action or a cheer
     - hype questions
     - mirrored slogans
     - lists of three by habit
     - stock phrases
     - named feelings
     - a tidy summing-up last line
     - sentences that all share one rhythm
   - Then run the normal clean-up pass (the Humanise rule and unslop).
7. For visuals:
   - Take the look from the subject's material, place, time or mood. Let one strong decision lead, with the rest serving it. Balance and centring are choices, not starting points.

- AI images give themselves away by their finish: smooth gradients, soft glow, perfect geometry, even spacing, one default font, the same polish everywhere. Replace that finish with the marks the chosen method leaves.
     - Print and paint: few inks, misregistration, uneven ink, paper grain.
     - Screens and machines: the pixel or dot grid, scan lines, colour banding.
     - Camera and science: grain, fall-off, blur, the instrument's false colours.
     - Material and light: seams, thickness, how the material reflects or glows.
   - Keep those marks real and sparse; a noise filter over a clean image fails. Don't add a hand-drawn wobble to a method that isn't made by hand.
   - Keep the working parts whole: text people must read, buttons people must press, the shape people must recognise. Roughness goes everywhere else.
   - Leave out any shape, glow, frame or icon that has no job.

8. For interfaces (app screens, dashboards, web pages):
   - The giveaway is the default shell: top bar with search, bell and avatar, sidebar, row of stat cards, rounded panels, one accent colour on a dark or white ground.
   - Change all three layers:
     - Layout: shape the page around the one question someone opens it to answer.
     - Method: let the method's own states (on and off, worn and new) carry the data.
     - Type and colour: one big statement beside small exact data, with colours that mean something.
   - Data still lines up, labels stay inside their areas, and buttons stay plain and pressable.
9. For ideas, names and options.
   - Skip the first idea in the field, the most famous mechanic, and the name made from the two most obvious words.
   - Make options that differ in kind. If one option is the safe pick, say so.

- End with one recommendation and its reason, not a long neutral list.
10. Watch for the escape turning into a default.
    - Signs it's happening:
      - an old, analogue or printed look chosen only because it reads as "not AI"
      - the same small palette, paper or texture from piece to piece
      - made-up names all from one stock (sea words, old trades, small English towns)
      - cream or off-white grounds
      - exact numbers used only to look concrete
      - a borrowed frame (a form, a map, a timetable) laid over the subject
      - a numbered label in the corner with a dry joke in the fine print
    - Keep a short log of the main move behind each off-default answer, a few plain words such as "poster: x-ray method, deep blue ground". Check it before showing new work. If the new piece shares its main move with the last one, pick another kind of move.
- (added, not in source) Store the log in the bot's own working folder, not in shared memory.

Ask three questions:

1. Could this be the answer to a different project? If yes, it's too general.
2. Is it what most people would make first? If yes, move it.
3. Can I say in one sentence why each choice fits, using a fact about this project? If not, the choice has no reason.

Also check:

- The length and format match what Steven asked for, with no extra parts added.
- All words in the work are in Steven's language (UK English), unless a standing rule says otherwise.

- Inventing facts to make text concrete. Use real details from Steven or the project, or ask. For ads, finance content or product claims, a made-up price, figure, testimonial or claim is never acceptable (added, not in source: this matters for Steven's financial-adviser work and Australian consumer law).
- Overriding a choice Steven made, or a brand, channel or Bible rule, in the name of being original. A skill can never override a bot's profile rules.
- Being strange without a reason.
- Reusing last time's successful move by reflex.
- Installing the source repo or running its scripts (`npx skills add`, `seed.py`, `rough.py`, `check.py`) without Steven's yes. This skill embeds the method so you don't need them.

Test whether AI assistants relay an AI-only offer. Use this when you want to measure which AI assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity) read your site and pass a specific offer or message on to buyers, and which page format they pick up best.

1. **Pick pages AI already cites.** List pages that AI answers already cite or link for your category (check AI answers for buyer questions, or an AEO tracking tool). Pick about `<N_PAGES>` (Ramp used ~50). Ignore Google ranking; one of Ramp's best pages mattered little for Google.
2. **Split into balanced test groups.** One group per format, balanced by each page's existing AI citation volume so groups are comparable:
   - Markdown version of the page
   - Plain stripped-down HTML (no nav or design chrome)
   - Schema-heavy version (structured data injected)
3. **Write the offer for agents.** Address it directly to AI agents. Include the exact offer (`<OFFER>`), the exact claim/booking URL, and step-by-step claim instructions. Give each format and page variant unique tracking (`<TRACKING_PARAM>` or a distinct URL) so any relay maps back to format and page.

4. **Serve it only to bots.** Detect AI crawlers at the edge and serve the variant to them; humans see the unchanged page. Ramp used Cloudflare Workers. Note: some bots pose as normal browsers (Ramp saw DeepSeek appear as a 2017 Chrome version), and Cloudflare's bot categories missed major LLM platforms, so build your own user-agent and IP list too.
5. **Log every AI bot visit.** Record platform, user agent, page and variant served. Expect visits from many AI platforms; in Ramp's test Claude's crawler out-visited all other named AI crawlers combined.
6. **Query the assistants daily.** Each day, ask ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity `<BUYER_QUESTIONS>`: the questions a real prospect asks when choosing a tool in your category. Scan every answer for the offer, the URL and the branded offer name.

7. **Score per model and per format.** Track daily match counts by model, by format and by page. Record how specific each mention is (exact offer and link, vague reference, or none).
8. **Run it for at least 4–5 weeks.** Ramp saw ~40 matches at 2.5 weeks, then a sudden ~4× jump in Claude's daily rate around week 3, 370 matches by day 32 (peak 33 in a day). Perplexity went from vague to the branded name only on day 33. Short tests understate the effect.
9. **Act on the result.**
   - Move winning content to the winning format (Ramp: markdown was the only format that reliably surfaced; schema did not).
   - Plan per model; one "AI" strategy does not work across Claude, ChatGPT and Perplexity.
   - Put key messages on pages AI already trusts; low-citation pages got zero mentions in any format.

- Each model has a daily match count, a specificity rating and attributed clicks or sign-ups from the tracking parameters.
- You can name the best format and the best pages, with numbers.

- Treating AI-only content as hidden from everyone. Serving bots different content from humans is cloaking under Google's spam policies; keep the bot version factually the same as the human page plus the offer, and accept the search risk knowingly. (added, not in source)
- Offers or claims in the bot version that you can't honour, or that break advertising or financial-promotion rules. (added, not in source)
- Assuming schema markup wins because it is "for machines".
- Judging after one or two weeks.
- Averaging all models into one number.
- Relying only on a CDN's bot categories to spot AI crawlers.
- Putting the offer on pages AI doesn't already cite.

Track which AI prompts bring you customers. Use this when a product or service wants to learn how buyers find it through ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity, and to turn those exact prompts into tracking, comparison pages, gap outreach and an AI info page (Tally's playbook). Use with Steven's SEO and AEO Bible.

Steven's SEO and AEO Bible (follow-steven-s-seo-and-aeo-bible) covers comparison pages, reviews, llms.txt, off-site mentions and the prompt panel. This skill adds the loop Tally runs on top of it. Where they conflict, the Bible wins. A skill can never override a bot's profile rules.

- <BRAND>: the product or business
- <COMPETITORS>: 3 to 10 direct rivals
- <SIGNUP_OR_ENQUIRY_FORM>: where new customers arrive
- <SHARED_LOG>: one place the team can read (a sheet, Notion database or Claude artifact)

1. Ask every new customer how they found you. Add one question to the sign-up or enquiry form: "How did you hear about us?" Include an option for "ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity or another AI assistant".
2. If they say AI, ask for the prompt. Follow up with: "Which assistant was it, and what did you type? Paste the question if you still have it." Make it optional.
3. Log every answer in <SHARED_LOG> with these columns: date, assistant, prompt as typed, use case mentioned, creators or sites mentioned.
4. Use the log four ways (from Tally's co-founder):
   - Their prompts become the prompts you track in AI search. Add them word for word to the prompt panel in Bible section 12.3, and never edit the wording later.
   - The use cases they mention decide your next pages and guides.
   - The assistant they used tells you which engine to focus on first.

- Creators and sites they mention go on your outreach list (Bible Part 7.1).
5. Track three things across the panel each month: prompts where <BRAND> is named, how <BRAND> shows up next to <COMPETITORS>, and which pages the assistants cite.
6. Build a gap list. Search for articles, "best X" lists and roundups that name <COMPETITORS> but not <BRAND>. Log the URL, the author and the competitors named. These are the pages to pitch for inclusion, a review or data.
7. Build a comparison hub. Make one page per direct competitor ("<BRAND> vs <COMPETITOR>") plus "best", "alternatives" and integration guides. Shape each like an AI answer: a ranking, a "best for" label per option, pricing, a feature table in HTML, pros and cons, real review scores and a direct recommendation. State honestly where a rival is the better pick. Refresh them on a schedule; the Bible says quarterly for comparisons.

8. Clear mentions daily. Monitor brand and competitor mentions on Reddit and in communities, route them into one shared inbox, and aim to clear it every day. Clearing means reading and deciding. Any public reply goes out under a named person, is drafted first, and needs approval (added, not in source).
9. Ask for reviews in two places: the newsletter, and right after a support conversation ends well. Never pay for or filter reviews.
10. Publish an AI info page. Write a plain page for assistants and people at a URL such as /ai-info. It says what <BRAND> is, who it's for, the main use cases, the pricing model, and what it doesn't do. Tally's version includes a visible "AI assistant guidelines" section listing the strengths, use cases and pricing to reference. Keep every line factual and visible to people, and link it from the footer.

11. Optional: llms.txt and agent access. Publish /llms.txt mapping product, pricing, customers, docs and API pages; the Bible notes that no major engine has confirmed using it, so treat it as cheap insurance. Tally also built an MCP server and ChatGPT and Claude apps so its product works inside the assistants. That's a product build and needs Steven's yes.

- At least 20 logged AI prompts within the first month of asking.
- Every logged prompt is in the tracking panel exactly as typed.
- The gap list has owners and dates, and the count of pages naming competitors but not <BRAND> is going down.
- The mention inbox is empty at the end of each day.

- Making the prompt question mandatory, or leading the answer by suggesting assistants first.
- Rewording a customer's prompt before tracking it. The exact wording is the point.
- Hidden text, or "guidelines" that tell an assistant to rank you first or to criticise rivals. The Bible's no-tricks rule bans prompt injection aimed at LLMs.
- Comparison pages that never admit a rival wins on anything; assistants cross-check against reviews.
- Replying in communities from fake or unnamed accounts, or posting a reply without approval.
- Incentivised, gated or fake reviews. In Australia that also breaches consumer law.
- For finance work such as Niche Connect: an AI info page or comparison page that makes claims about returns or outcomes. These need a compliance check first (added, not in source).
- Copying Tally's growth numbers into a pitch as if they were yours, or as expected results.
- Letting this skill override a bot's profile rules. It can't.

Treat verification as critical infrastructure. Use this when creating or maintaining an agent verification skill with pstack (/create-verification-skill, Build the Lever CLI, Feature Map, /maintain-verification-skill), preferring cloud agents over worktrees, or using verification in feature/perf/feedback loops.

1. Treat a high-quality verification skill as critical infrastructure (not "just" a skill): an agent that can verify its own work closes the loop without you as the bottleneck. Done well, it can amplify whole-team output (including non-engineers).
2. Install pstack, then run `/create-verification-skill`. Optionally add Dr Eggbot (ships with pstack) and ask it to create an engineer bot that runs `/create-verification-skill` and sets up a daily routine for `/maintain-verification-skill`.

3. Prefer a tech stack / runtime that agents can interact with and debug (e.g. Electron/web via Chrome DevTools Protocol; iOS simulator). If the runtime is poor, ask the agent to create tools (e.g. lldb, or a custom sidecar package) or use what you have — [PLACEHOLDER: exact tool list for your stack]. Agentic verification is important enough that building rich debugging tools or choosing a different stack may be worth it.
4. Apply "Build the Lever": prefer giving agents tools rather than just markdown. For verification, create a small CLI that scripts interaction and debugging of your app in an agent-friendly utility (fewer tokens than throwaway click scripts; more reproducible and testable).
5. Design the agent-friendly CLI with these properties (from the extract):
   - API easy to compose (deep modules)
   - Potentially destructive commands have `--dry-run`

- Subcommands for gradual disclosure
   - Descriptive error messages that say what to do instead
   - Rich `--help` text
   - Machine-readable output (e.g. JSON)
6. Also cover dev experience the CLI should support: seeding a dev database; auth / test users / API calls against test/staging; installing and bringing up the dev environment consistently. Keep the CLI well maintained and tested. Spend time making it good and error-free before advanced work. Hypothetical Electron CLI command examples: [PLACEHOLDER — media in source; not transcribed]. Other example commands: [PLACEHOLDER — media in source; not transcribed].
7. Prefer Cursor cloud agents over local git worktrees for parallelism after the verification skill can land a few PRs:
   - Worktrees: high storage/resources; limited parallel agents on one machine.

- Cloud agents: real computer; install deps; run app; videos/screenshots; interact like a user. Set up cloud environment (first-build agent help; then snapshot for fast subsequent starts). [PLACEHOLDER: exact cloud environment setup commands for your repo].
8. Create a Feature Map (searchable map of features, what they do, how to get there from a user's perspective):
   - `/create-verification-skill` auto-creates `references/features` alongside a README.md (the map: high-level overview with links to details). Mention Feature Map files in the verification SKILL.md.
   - Agents catalog the app for you — don't write these yourself initially.
   - Treat as "materialized memory": compact form of codebase truth designed to save tokens; shared markdown inside the skill benefits all contributors.

- Example feature entry shape: [PLACEHOLDER — media in source; not transcribed]. Example verification skill: https://github.com/poteto/verification-skill-example
9. Maintain continuously: run `/maintain-verification-skill` at least once a day so agents have latest control details. Agents may update Feature Map while working; `/maintain-verification-skill` catches what is missed. Keep improving the CLI; invest like critical infra (optional: oncall rotation on it).
10. Usage patterns (with `/poteto-mode`; in Cursor, Opt+Enter on autocomplete can pin `/poteto-mode` as a Custom Mode so the agent is reminded every turn):

- New features: `/poteto-mode build <description of feature, any useful context>. use /control-app to verify your changes and show me a video and screenshots as proof` (`/control-app` = result of `/create-verification-skill`). In Grok @Bot: spawn a cloud agent to do the same (keeps bot context clean; bot as coordinator).
    - Perf: `spawn a cloud agent to use /poteto-mode to improve the initial loading time of our app. first use /control-app to take a trace of the status quo, and identify opportunities for improvement. then do a targeted fix and use /control-app + a /swarm to confirm the win` (`/swarm` fans out cloud agents to run verification for sample size / fuzz / no-regression).

- User reports: put verification inside Grok @Bot routines or Cursor Automations (schedule or event). Pipe feedback (e.g. Slack); bots try to reproduce with a cloud agent; if Feature Map/verification is good enough, optionally auto-fix.

- Treating verification as a one-off skill instead of maintained infrastructure.
- Giving agents only markdown instead of a Build-the-Lever CLI.
- Jumping to advanced verification before the CLI is good and error-free.
- Preferring local worktrees for multi-agent parallelism when cloud agents are available after a solid verification/dev setup.
- Letting the Feature Map go stale (skip daily `/maintain-verification-skill`).
- Choosing/keeping a tech stack that is hard to debug and control without investing in agent-usable tooling.

Turn launch-post replies into personalized product demos. Use this when launching a product on X whose output can be personalized (video, image, copy, audit) and you want the reply section to become a live demo that drives signups.

X ranks posts that keep people on the platform. Long reply threads and time spent in the comments push a post further. Every personalized result posted in the replies is a public demo, which makes the next person ask for one too.

1. **Pick the personalization.** Choose one thing your product can make for a single person in about a minute: [OUTPUT, e.g. a video of them in a movie scene].
2. **Write the hook reply.** Answer "congrats"-type comments with a question that collects the input. Example: "Thanks! What's your favorite movie? I'll make you something cool."
3. **Wire the pipeline:**
   - The X API reads new replies on the launch post.
   - Claude turns each reply (plus profile context) into a generation prompt: [PROMPT_TEMPLATE].
   - [PRODUCT_API] generates the result.
   - The X API posts a reply with a preview and a link.
4. **Gate the full result.** Reply "Your [OUTPUT]'s ready, go check it out" with a preview and a link to [RESULT_PAGE]. The full result is waiting on your site, and editing or keeping it requires signing up.

5. **Personalize onboarding.** After signup, tailor the experience to their name, company and what they asked for.
6. **Let it compound.** Every public preview invites more requests. Watch the comment-to-like ratio and time in the replies as signs it's working.

- Only use someone's photo or likeness if they explicitly asked, and say upfront what you'll make.
- Automated replies should go only to people who replied to you. Rate-limit them, avoid duplicate text, and follow X's automation rules and API tier limits.
- Have a human review outputs before they post, and plan capacity, since the source says launches have broken products under load.
The source's 10-page setup guide is gated. Exact X API endpoints, prompt templates and queue design are [PLACEHOLDER].
Products with no fast, personalizable output, or cold auto-replies to people who didn't engage.

Turn PR smells into lasting rules. Use this when acting as codebase gardener — watching the PR stream for recurring smells and converting each weed into a rule or hard constraint so agent-era slop cannot grow back.

1. Assign (or act as) a gardener: someone quietly watching the stream of PRs into the codebase, noticing smells (examples from the extract: the third `isRecord` this week; lint suppressions creeping like ivy).
2. Tend weeds steadily: every weed you pull becomes a rule so it cannot grow back. With careful grooming the codebase stays a garden; without that, it is just whatever grew.
3. Prefer organic architecture foundations over soft guidance alone:
   - Good codebases have strong foundations and constraints (these files go here; this kind of code goes there) — historically via conventional frameworks/languages for the lowest common denominator, or a style guide enforced by code review.
   - Infinite agent "monkeys with keyboards" obsolete style-guide-only enforcement. Codebases designed for agents need hard constraints so even the dumbest agent (and pilot) can contribute meaningfully.

4. Invest where impact is highest (per extract): refactoring the codebase and choosing a tech stack with strong type systems / compiler diagnostics has far greater impact than AGENTS.md and tweaking skills. Hard constraints and well thought-out architecture guide agents to do the right thing by default. The best rules are in your code.
5. Encode each recurring smell as a durable constraint — [PLACEHOLDER: lint rule / type / CI check / compiler diagnostic chosen for your stack] — so the same weed cannot return.

- Leaving PR smells unchecked until the garden is engulfed in slop.
- Relying mainly on AGENTS.md and skill tweaks instead of hard constraints, architecture, and typed/compiler-backed rules in code.
- Expecting code review style guides alone to tame agent-scale contribution volume.

Warehouse Meta ads; API for mutations only. Use this when Meta/Facebook Ads MCP or Marketing API work is burning tokens or hitting rate limits — analyze from a warehouse and reserve the API for account mutations only.

1. Assume Facebook/Meta Ads MCP ultimately hits the same Meta Marketing API rate limits as direct API use. Broad account scans, parallel agent calls, bulk changes, and retry loops can exhaust per-account quota or trigger throttling and burn tokens.
2. Stop using the live Ads API/MCP as your analytics store. Ingest ad account data into a [DATA_WAREHOUSE] on a schedule (or via your existing ETL).
3. Run all analysis, reporting, and exploration against the warehouse — not against live MCP “list everything” calls.
4. Restrict Marketing API / Ads MCP traffic to **mutations only**: create/upload ads, turn ads on/off, budget changes, and other account updates you intentionally approve.
5. When agents need context for a change, pull the needed rows from the warehouse first, then issue a narrow API update. Avoid retry storms; back off on throttle responses.
6. Optional: use a managed sync/warehouse layer (source mentions graphed.com/platform) if you do not already have ETL — not required for the pattern.

- Analysis queries never hammer Meta’s API
- API/MCP calls are mostly writes you meant to make
- Token burn and rate-limit errors drop after warehouse cutover

- Parallel agents scanning full ad accounts via MCP for “insights”
- Bulk dry-run style reads that still consume quota
- Treating Ads MCP as a free data lake
- Not a Graphed sales pitch — warehouse + mutation-only API is the method

Willow Phase YouTube playbook. Use this when Willow Phase packages, schedules, reviews or measures an ambient music single on YouTube, to know which saved YouTube skills apply, how to adapt them to short instrumental releases, and which tactics to skip.

The live profile holds the job, the channel facts and the approval gates. This file maps the YouTube methods Steven has saved onto ambient music singles. Pull the named skill when a step needs its detail.

| Job | Skill | Use | Skip or adapt |
|---|---|---|---|
| Channel setup, About, banner, launch trio | plan-a-youtube-channel-with-nine-production-prom, step 2 | promise line, banner under 8 words, three linked launch videos | niche and script steps 1, 3 and 5 are for talking videos |
| Title and thumbnail | same skill, step 6, plus pod-satire-virality-playbook, Packaging | title, thumbnail and first frame make the same promise; thumb text at most 4 words, one subject, high contrast; no misleading packaging | the proof is the mood and the place (the nature shot), not a demo |
| Pre-publish check | same skill, step 7 | reused or repetitive material, rights, AI disclosure, missed promises | run it on every release, batch or not |
| Release promo off YouTube | run-a-music-release-promo-checklist | rights and metadata phase, track story and core emotion, targets set before any spend, value-first Reddit and Discord, T+4 review | draft only; posting, DMs, email and paid lines need Steven's yes per item |
| Analytics | same plan skill, step 8, plus pod-satire-virality-playbook, Metric mapping | compare same-format uploads at similar ages; label hypothesis versus measured | no verdict from private or prelaunch views |
| Monetisation | same plan skill, step 9 | check official YouTube Help, separate fan funding from ads | no fixed window, no revenue forecasts |
| Shorts | same plan skill, step 10, plus ship-30-identical-shorts, levers 3 to 5 | a 15 to 30 second loop of the strongest section of the track, a distinct first frame, ending on the payoff, linked to the full single | no voiceover or captions script; own audio only |
| Visual openers | build-an-ai-hook-bank-from-saved-tiktoks | save visual first frames that stop the scroll; remap the pattern | no spoken hooks; never copy |
| Study a reference channel or video | hand off to the YouTube Blueprint bot | a plan for an original take | never clone |

1. Name the listening purpose for each single (focus, wind-down, walking, background) and put it in the title or the first description line. A 3 to 5 minute single does a different job from an hour-long mix, so don't package it like one.
2. Titles: track name first, then a plain mood or setting cue. Example: "Field Margins · ambient techno with summer meadow footage". No hype words.
3. Description: line 1 is the mood and purpose; then the track family, the tempo or feel if known, and the AI-music disclosure wording Steven approved. Add playlist and next-single links once they exist. Add no footage credits or sources.
4. Use one playlist per track family plus a full-releases playlist in release order. End screens point to the next single or the family playlist.
5. A later compilation mix made only from released singles is an option. Flag the reused-content risk and let Steven decide.

6. Vary the footage and colour treatment between tracks. A strict identical template across 26 AI-music uploads is the pattern the inauthentic-content policy targets, so don't borrow ship-30-identical-shorts' fixed template for the long-form singles.

- From run-a-multi-channel-shorts-network: burner channels, rival pairs, comment seeding from second accounts, fake first comments. Only its account-hygiene step applies (roles for editors, 2FA, current recovery email).
- Engagement bait, sub4sub, fake giveaways, or misleading thumbnails.
- Monetisation timelines, CTR scores or revenue numbers that are not from Studio or official pages.

- Compare each single at 7 and 28 days against the others at the same ages.
- Long-form: impressions click-through rate (CTR), average percentage viewed, returning viewers, and playlist adds. Shorts: stayed-to-watch rate and the click-through to the linked single.
- CTR and impressions come from a Studio Advanced-mode CSV export. Willow Phase has no Markifact or Metricool connection.
- Wait for at least 6 to 8 singles before changing the format. One weak upload is noise.

Win long-tail AI recommendations with narrow Q&A pages. Use this when a new or small brand can't break into AI assistants' answers for broad "best X" questions and you want to get named for narrow, problem-specific questions instead, measure which assistants pick it up, and optionally scale the winners into many pages with AI.

1. **Skip the head terms.** The 3 to 5 brands an assistant names for broad asks ("best `<CATEGORY>`", "cheapest", "`<COMMON_FEATURE>`-free") barely moved over 6 to 7 months of Burke's tracking. Don't target them first.
2. **Pick 4 or 5 narrow buyer problems.** Each one is a specific problem plus a specific constraint, phrased the way a buyer would ask an assistant. Burke's example: "I get irritation from baking soda. What natural deodorant should I buy for sensitive skin?" Write yours as `<LONG_TAIL_QUESTIONS>`.
3. **Name the specific terms.** Put the exact ingredients, features, methods or comparisons those questions involve (Burke used "colloidal oatmeal" and "magnesium hydroxide") into the copy, word for word.
4. **Build a small site and get it indexed.** Burke used a $11.25 domain, a site Claude built on Vercel in about 20 minutes, and 3 pages:

- a product or service page with specifics (her "formulation notes")
   - product Q&A pages that answer the narrow questions directly
   - one comparison page for the narrow choice (hers: magnesium vs baking soda for sensitive skin)
5. **Publish one off-site essay in the brand's voice.** Burke posted one Substack essay bylined as the brand. She wrote no reviews or testimonials and paid for no coverage.
6. **Query on a schedule and leave it alone.** Run a script that asks each assistant the long-tail questions plus about 13 broad control questions. Ask ChatGPT with browsing on and with browsing off, Claude and Gemini. Log whether the brand is named and in what position. Burke didn't touch the site for 30 days.
7. **Read the results by assistant and by query.** In Burke's test:
   - ChatGPT with browsing on named the brand first in 4 of 4 long-tail answers, starting at week 3.

- ChatGPT with browsing off: not named.
   - The 13 broad questions: not named.
   - Claude and Gemini: never named it.
8. **Double down on what got picked up.** Add more Q&A and comparison pages for the narrow questions that worked. Keep testing the others per assistant. (added, not in source)

9. **Mine real pain points.** Have the AI review competitors' data and best pages in bulk and pull out users' real pain points. gkxspace built for a need he had himself, so he knew what good looked like.
10. **Generate pages for every narrow question.** Have Claude generate pages in bulk (he made over a thousand), one per finely split question, each targeting a different audience and need, each with an overview section and Q&A. He found ChatGPT's crawler picked up new pages very fast.
11. **Attribute, then let the AI maintain it in a loop.** Track which pages are indexed and which bring revenue. Have the AI:
    - improve the pages that convert best
    - fix or remove pages that aren't indexed or have problems
    - expand the topics that sell most
    Rerun the loop on a schedule. He says he stepped in only a few times.

- A per-assistant table of the long-tail and broad questions, showing named or not, with position, checked weekly for at least 4 weeks.
- The brand is named for at least one narrow question on at least one assistant.
- If scaled: indexed pages, AI-referred visits and revenue per page, so the maintenance loop has numbers to act on.

chunks.section: Example for a golf pro (added, not in source)
chunks.text:
- `<LONG_TAIL_QUESTIONS>`: "I'm over 50 and keep slicing my driver. Should I book lessons or a fitting near `<SUBURB>`?" or "Is a playing lesson or a range lesson better for breaking 90?"
- Pages: the lesson offer with specifics, a Q&A page per question, and one comparison page (for example, playing lesson vs range lesson).

- Inventing a brand, product, credentials or ingredients to sell. Burke's brand was fake on purpose to prove a point. Use real offers and true claims only. (added, not in source)
- Fake reviews or testimonials. Burke used none, and they break consumer law. (added, not in source)
- In regulated niches such as finance, health or advice, publishing Q&A answers without a compliance check. (added, not in source)
- Thousands of near-identical AI pages with nothing useful on them. Google's spam policies call mass-produced, low-value pages "scaled content abuse", and that can sink the whole site in search. Each page should answer its question with real specifics. (added, not in source)

- Letting the AI delete pages or data unattended. Keep deletes behind a human check and a backup. One of gkxspace's screenshots shows Claude stopping before a database delete because it found real paying users. (added, not in source)
- Judging the result on "best X" queries.
- Treating "AI" as one channel. Pickup differed completely between ChatGPT with browsing, ChatGPT without it, Claude and Gemini.
- Checking once in week 1 and giving up. Pickup took about 3 weeks.

Write a cold-traffic ad from a 17-element brief. Use this when writing a direct-response video ad or VSL script for cold traffic (people who don't know the brand) and you need to work out what to say, in what order, before writing.

chunks.section: Write a cold-traffic ad from a 17-element brief
chunks.text: Derick Carneiro's method for direct-response video ads aimed at people who don't know the brand. The ad has to make four "sales" before the product is pitched: the content, hope, value and impulse sales. Each sale is built from "reasons why" the viewer already wants to hear, and there are 17 of them in total. You find those reasons from facts about the product and from ads that are already winning, fill them into a brief, then write the brief into the structure of a proven reference ad.

Stage 1, the content sale (make them want to watch to the end):
1. Format: why the viewer relaxes and doesn't suspect a sales pitch.
2. Topic: why the viewer might care about what the ad says.
3. Concept: why they feel they have to watch to the end.
4. Visual hook: why they snap out of autopilot and stop scrolling.
5. Copy hook: why they decide to keep watching.

Stage 2, the hope sale (why it failed before and why this works):
6. Identification: why they feel understood.
7. Point of contact: what they already suspect causes the problem.
8. Unique mechanism of the problem: the missing reason that proves their suspicion right.
9. Unique mechanism of the function: the action needed to fix it, and why other solutions can't do it.
10. Unique mechanism of the solution: the one thing that performs that action, with proof.

11. Conditions: why other solutions don't offer it, and what makes it rare or hard to get.

Stage 3, the value sale (why this product):
12. Unique selling proposition: why this product is the best or only place to get the mechanism under the right conditions.
13. Features: only the components that raise the odds of the result, make the dream outcome tangible, cut effort or shorten the timeline.
14. Anchoring: why not solving the problem costs more (money, emotion, time) than the price.

Stage 4, the impulse sale (why now):
15. Risk reversal: why not buying is riskier than buying.
16. What they gain by buying now.
17. What they lose by waiting.

1. Premises. List the facts you already have from the product page: brand, product, ingredients or components, attributes, price and bundles, guarantee, what buyers gain by buying now, and what they lose by waiting. Use only real facts.
2. Pick the market (a group sharing one desire). For a running brand, use the market its highest-traffic landing pages and most-launched ads of the last 60 days target. For an untested product, list the markets it could serve, drop any with fewer than three competitors, and pick the one whose competitors grew traffic most in the last 30 days. He uses the GetHookd ad library (with its MCP and Claude) and TrendTrack for this. Don't gamble on a new market: save the risk for concept, format and hook.

3. Pick the segment: a cluster within the market that shares a condition, identity or behaviour. Either reuse the segment that winning ads (yours or competitors') already target, or read Reddit threads to find one nobody is targeting.
4. Profile the avatar in two layers.
   - Psychographics: primary desire, main problem, secondary desires, pain points, dreams, fears. Take these from winning ads, funnels and past sales letters in the same market rather than doing days of fresh research. They barely change over time.
   - Identity: demographics; behaviour (which competitor ads, videos, trends, hobbies, news and shows catch their attention, and any related conditions); perspective (beliefs, biases, enemies, allies, language). Put most of your research effort into behaviour, because that's where topics, formats, concepts and hooks come from.

5. Brief the mechanism by answering four questions. Which point of contact does this avatar want to hear? Which problem mechanism are they most ready to accept? Which function mechanism? Which solution mechanism? Connect dots they already believe rather than teaching something new.
6. Brief the content.
   - Topic: list candidate facts, topics or situations the avatar cares about, using search demand and what winning ads cover, then pick one.
   - Format: the look, narrative style and characters, with their roles. Reuse elements from ads already performing, and place at most one deliberate new bet.
   - Concept: combine characters, narrative and topic into a one-line logline, then find the angle that makes the avatar need to hear more.
   - Copy hook: pick a hook structure that's proven in ad libraries and fits the concept, then write it.

- Visual hook: something that fits the format and concept but breaks expectations.
7. Brief the offer.
   - Conditions: answer "why can't I just get this myself?"
   - Unique selling proposition: show that the product meets each of those conditions, one by one, using only facts from the premises.
   - Features: map each one to odds, dream, effort or time, and drop any that map to none.
   - Anchoring: compare the daily price with the money, emotional and time cost of not solving the problem.
8. Brief the close. Risk reversal (for example, a guarantee longer than the time results take), the gain from buying now (bundles, shipping), and the loss from waiting. Use only real deadlines and stock limits.

9. Write. Download and transcribe a proven reference ad in the same market. Split it into mini-blocks by job (hook, belief break, mechanism reveal, product presentation and so on), then fill each block from the brief. You can do this by hand, or give a writing model the brief and the reference's block structure. The brief decides what gets said. The reference only decides the order and the rhythm.
10. Batch by risk. Each new bet (concept, format, hook, segment) raises an ad's risk. For a scaling brand, run a few conservative ads, many moderate ones and some aggressive ones.
11. Success check (added, not in source): every one of the 17 elements is filled in the brief with a reason, each factual claim traces back to a premise, and the script follows the reference's block order.

- Opening a cold-traffic ad with price, product or offer.
- Letting AI write the ad without a brief. He says this is why most AI-written ads fail.
- Listing ingredients or features that don't serve odds, dream, effort or time.
- Spending days on psychographic research that winning ads already contain, while neglecting behaviour research.
- Betting on a new market when the gain is in a new concept, format or hook.
- Promising fast results the avatar has stopped believing.

- (Added, not in source.) Making health, medical, income or financial claims that the product page and the law don't support. His worked example is a capsaicin supplement for men with diabetes and erectile dysfunction, using a sexualised video-game character and a Black Friday "stock running out" close. Platform ad policies and consumer law in Australia and elsewhere restrict health claims, sexual content and false scarcity. For Niche Connect or any financial-adviser client, financial-promotion rules apply too. Check every claim before an ad runs.

Write LinkedIn posts that collect leads, not likes. Use this when a B2B company or founder wants LinkedIn posts that book sales calls, and needs a post type, a fill-in template and a lead-magnet plan.
Write the post your buyer would ask you to send them.

1. Give away the work: a finished thing usable the same day (skill pack, guide, checklist, template, repo, teardown).
2. Prove you used it yourself: name who on your team uses it and what it did for you.
3. Filter fast: line 1 states the problem or result so only your buyer stops. Everyone else scrolls.

- <LEAD_MAGNET>: a finished asset you use yourself
- <BUYER>: who you sell to
- <PROOF_NUMBER>: a real figure from your own work
- <EMAIL_CAPTURE_PAGE>: a page that asks for an email, not a comment

1. Pick one post type below. Start with the behind-the-scenes demo.
2. Build one lead magnet you use yourself, finished and usable the same day.
3. Write line 1 for your buyer, with the proof or the problem in it.
4. Put the result or offer in line 2.
5. Link to <EMAIL_CAPTURE_PAGE> in the post. Don't ask for a comment word: the author reports LinkedIn now cuts reach on those (his test: 32 impressions in 18 minutes; unverified).
6. Follow up with people who fit while they still remember you. The author says signups without follow-up were wasted.
7. Track signups, meetings booked and revenue from content. Likes come last.
8. Reuse your best lead magnet about 3 months later with a new first line. Share it on X and YouTube too.

1. Behind-the-scenes demo: show your best person doing what you sell, with their exact tools. Order: person, result, list of jobs and tools.
```
<Name>, our <role>, <does the thing you sell> at <a real number>.
<What it changed for your business, in 1 line.>

What <the setup> does every week:
→ <job 1>
→ <job 2>
→ <job 3>

<The tools it runs on.>
Get the setup free: <EMAIL_CAPTURE_PAGE>
```
2. Guide that picks a fight: topic is the question your buyer asks right before they need you. Open with something they already dislike. Three bullets answer three objections (one per reader type). Show the result before the contents.
```
Rest in peace, <the thing your buyer is tired of>.
For 2026, I built <the guide> so you can <the result they want>.

→ <Objection 1, answered>
→ <Objection 2, answered>
→ <Objection 3, answered>

What our team got with it: <the result>.
What's inside: <the contents>
Get it free: <EMAIL_CAPTURE_PAGE>
```
3. Tool post: build something inside a tool your buyers use daily, then name every file or piece.
```
I built <what you built> that <result 1>, <result 2> and <result 3>, all inside <the tool your buyers use>.

The <N> files we use ourselves:
1. <name>
2. <name>
3. <name>
Get them free: <EMAIL_CAPTURE_PAGE>
```
4. Shift post: name what is changing in your buyer's job now. Old way in one line, new way in one line, then one step per line.
```
<The job> used to mean <the old way>.
<Who> do it like this now:
→ <step 1>
→ <step 2>
→ <step 3>
Get <the free thing that does step 1>: <EMAIL_CAPTURE_PAGE>
```

5. "My team didn't want me to share this": one-line story with tension, contents sorted by team or role, then say what it doesn't need (no setup, keys or code).
```
My team didn't want me to share this: <the thing we use for the job>.

For <team 1>: <item>
For <team 2>: <item>
For <team 3>: <item>

No setup. Copy it straight into <the tool they already use>.
Get it free: <EMAIL_CAPTURE_PAGE>
```
6. Link post: proof in line 1, offer in line 2, link to the email page, no comment word.
```
We packaged <N> <things> that <proof number> at <your company>.
Get them for free, ready to <use them>.

<What's inside, 1 line per item.>

<EMAIL_CAPTURE_PAGE>
```

- Signups, meetings booked and revenue from content are tracked per post.
- A post can be judged a win with few likes if signups are high (the author's post #6: 186 likes, 142 day-one signups).

- Posts with no asset behind them (the author's 2,400-like post produced 0 leads).
- Comment-word bait as the only capture method.
- Lead magnets that were generated and never used by your team.
- Collecting emails and never following up.
- Emailing or messaging signups beyond what they consented to; follow local email and privacy law. (added, not in source)
- Treating the author's counts as a benchmark for your account.
